And he says, [[1:11|stretch forth thy hand a little|Extende paululum]], because whatever harm the devil does to a man, so long as he has not hurt and deceived his soul, he thinks he has done little. Satan also meant to prove that Job was in no way truly just, but only in pretence, by saying, [[1:11|stretch forth thy hand a little|Extende paululum]]. For to be troubled by a small adversity, or by the taking away of outward things, is the mark of those who are just in pretence: for the perfect and truly just do not fall into impatience even for an injury to their own body. It can also be explained, according to Thomas, with *bless* taken in its proper sense; and the sense will be: [[1:11|touch all that he hath, and see if he bless thee not to thy face|Tange quæ possidet, nisi in facie benedixerit tibi]], that is, may evil befall me unless it be plain that in the time of prosperity he blessed thee not truly in his heart but to thy face, that is, in appearance and before the eyes of men.

paras.t: Sed quum diabolus certissime sciat Deum esse veracem, nec posse mentiri, quomodo contradicere potuit verbis ipsius? Et respondendum, quod non putavit verba Dei esse mendosa, sed stimulante ipsum sua invidia, non timuit proferre mendacium, quum ab initio sit mendax, et pater ejus. Possunt etiam præinducta ita intelligi, quod diabolus scivit ex propria consideratione et magis ex verbis Dei sanctum Job esse veraciter timoratum, et quod temporalium affluentia esset ei occasio magis timendi Deum; nec tamen putavit eum tam justum, quin ex temporalium sublatione tentationi succumberet et peccaret. Denique Satan non prius a Domino expetiit ipsum Job ad tentandum, ut ait Gregorius; sed quum Dominus in despectum Satan laudasset Job, tunc irritatus diabolus petiit tentandi licentiam. Quum equidem superbissimus sit, metuit a viris virtutum devinci: et in hoc consideranda dispensatio pietatis ac sapientiæ Dei, præbentis diabolo occasionem impugnandi justos, quos Deus prænoscit victuros, et ex prælio cum Satana amplius coronandos.
paras.en: But since the devil knows most certainly that God is truthful and cannot lie, how could he contradict his words? It is to be answered that he did not think God's words false, but, goaded by his envy, he did not fear to utter a lie, since from the beginning he [[John 8:44|is a liar, and the father thereof|mendax, et pater ejus]]. The foregoing can also be understood thus: the devil knew by his own observation, and still more from God's words, that holy Job was truly God-fearing, and that the abundance of temporal things was for him an occasion of fearing God the more; yet he did not think him so just that he would not give way to temptation and sin when temporal things were taken from him. Lastly, Satan did not first ask the Lord for Job, to tempt him, as Gregory says; but when the Lord had praised Job in contempt of Satan, then the devil, provoked, asked leave to tempt him. For since he is most proud, he dreads being overcome by men of virtue: and herein is to be considered the dispensation of God's mercy and wisdom, which gives the devil occasion to attack the just, who, as God foreknows, will conquer, and will be crowned the more for their battle with Satan.

paras.t: Dixit ergo Dominus ad Satan, id est adversarium salutis humanæ: Ecce universa quæ habet, in manu tua sunt, id est, potestati tibi a me collatæ tangenda dissipandaque trado sive permitto. Voluntatem autem nocendi habes, o Satan, a te: sed potestas omnis a me est; abusio autem potestatis, ex tua est perversitate. Hinc dicit Gregorius: Satanæ voluntas semper iniqua est, sed potestas ejus nunquam injusta: quia a semetipso voluntatem habet (id est impiam ultionem, non volitivam potentiam), sed a Domino potestatem. Tantum in eum ne extendas manum tuam, id est, ipsum in propria persona non tangas nec lædas. Quo liquet, tantum et non amplius posse diabolum in nos, quantum a Deo permittitur. Propter quod ait Apostolus: Fidelis Dominus, qui non patietur vos tentari supra id quod potestis. Imo nec in ea quæ attinent homini seu possidentur ab eo, plus potest quam Deus permittit; unde legio dæmonum dixit ad Christum: Si ejicis nos, permitte nos intrare in porcos. Deus ergo refrenat tyrannidem dæmonis, et potestatem ipsius coarctat, prout condecens novit, et homines ferre posse conspectat.
paras.en: [[1:12|Then the Lord said to Satan|Dixit ergo Dominus ad Satan]], that is, to the adversary of man's salvation: [[1:12|Behold, all that he hath is in thy hand|Ecce universa quæ habet, in manu tua sunt]], that is, I hand them over, or permit them, to the power given thee by me, to be touched and scattered. The will to harm, O Satan, thou hast from thyself; but all power is from me; and the abuse of the power comes from thy perversity. Hence Gregory says: Satan's will is always wicked, but his power is never unjust: for he has the will from himself (that is, the impious act of willing, not the power of willing [the text prints *ultionem*, 'vengeance', with a note giving *volitionem*, 'act of willing', which the sense requires]), but the power from the Lord. [[1:12|only put not forth thy hand upon his person|Tantum in eum ne extendas manum tuam]], that is, do not touch or hurt him in his own person. From this it is clear that the devil can do as much against us as God permits, and no more. For which reason the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 10:13|God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that which you are able|Fidelis Dominus, qui non patietur vos tentari supra id quod potestis]]. Nay, even over the things that belong to a man or are possessed by him, he has no more power than God permits; whence the legion of devils said to Christ: [[Matt 8:31|If thou cast us out|Si ejicis nos]], suffer us to enter into the swine[[Luke 8:32||]]. God therefore curbs the devil's tyranny and restrains his power, as he knows to be fitting, and as he sees that men are able to bear.

paras.t: Circa prædicta scribit Albertus: Ea quæ dicta sunt, Judæi et nostri judaizantes hæretici, aliter exponunt, dicentes, quod in die, id est in luce, divinæ providentiæ, angeli seu filii Dei, id est bonæ creaturæ et secundum rectum intellectum agentes, Deo adsistunt; malæ autem creaturæ, quæ significantur per Satan, ut sensualitas inclinans ad malum, etiam adsunt: et hoc esse quod dicitur omnis homo habere bonum angelum a dextris, et malum a sinistris. Et ideo, quoniam malum est infinitum, quærere Dominum per verbum infinitum: Unde venis? et Satan, id est materiam cum privatione, dicere: Circuivi terram, undique spargendo malum privationis: in cœlo enim non habet locum, quia ibi non est generatio neque corruptio. Quod autem Dominus ait, Numquid considerasti, etc.? et dæmon, Extende, etc., est quædam etiam incorruptibilia ad corruptionem et perversitatem appetere, ut quod in fabula Phaethontis dicit Ovidius, quod Phaeton male dirigens cursum solis, combussit cœlum et terram, intelligens hoc de exorbitatione planetarum, per comparationem ad medium quod est terra, vel etiam de perversitate recti hominis per malitiam privationis, vel de malitia periodi declinantis ad domum infaustam: cui datur licentia, quando infaustis fausti prævalent. Et hoc colligitur in tertia Collatione Rabbi Moysis in libro qui dicitur, Dux neutrorum, capitulo vicesimo quarto. Quam opinionem sequuntur Abraham, Isaac et Moyses Ægyptius, Judæorum philosophi, eo quod dicant angelos intelligentias esse, quæ sint ubique et semper, et nusquam mittantur; angelos autem qui mittuntur, effectus eorum esse in inferioribus, vel homines qui corde præsago ista prænuntiant, sive ad bonum sive ad malum. Prima autem expositio secundum catholicam veritatem est, et alterius opinionis sive erroris fabulam non curamus. Hucusque Albertus.
paras.en: On the foregoing Albert writes: The Jews, and our judaizing heretics, expound what has been said otherwise. They say that in the day, that is, in the light, of divine providence, the angels or sons of God, that is, good creatures, acting according to right understanding, stand before God; while evil creatures, which are signified by Satan, such as sensuality inclining to evil, are present too: and that this is the meaning of the saying that every man has a good angel at his right hand and an evil one at his left[[Ps 90:11||]] [the margin gives Ps. xc, with a verse number that cannot be read; v. 11 speaks of the angels given charge over us]. And therefore, since evil is indefinite, the Lord asks with an indefinite word [*infinitum* in both places: evil, being privation, has no definite form, and *whence* names no definite place]: [[1:7|Whence comest thou?|Unde venis?]] and Satan, that is, matter with privation, says: [[1:7|I have gone round about the earth|Circuivi terram]], spreading the evil of privation everywhere: for in heaven it has no place, since there is neither generation nor corruption there. And as for the Lord's saying, [[1:8|Hast thou considered|Numquid considerasti]], etc.? and the demon's, [[1:11|stretch forth|Extende]], etc., this means that even some incorruptible things desire corruption and perversity; as Ovid says in the fable of Phaethon that Phaeton, steering the course of the sun badly, burned heaven and earth: understanding this of the planets' going out of their orbits, by comparison with the middle, which is the earth; or else of the perversion of an upright man through the malice of privation; or of the malice of a period declining to an unlucky house [a term of astrology], to which leave is given when the lucky prevail over the unlucky. And this is gathered from the third Collation of Rabbi Moses, in the book called the Guide of the Perplexed [Latin *Dux neutrorum*: the work of Moses Maimonides], chapter twenty-four. This opinion is followed by Abraham, Isaac and Moses the Egyptian, philosophers of the Jews, because they say that the angels are intelligences which are everywhere and always, and are never sent; and that the angels who are sent are their effects in lower things, or men who with a presaging heart foretell these things, whether for good or for evil. But the first exposition is according to Catholic truth, and we take no account of the fable of the other opinion, or rather error. Thus far Albert.

paras.t: Præterea Deus perfectionem justorum vult omnibus esse notam, ideo voluit etiam intentionem sancti Job, omnibus justam ostendere per patientiam suam in adversis: propter quod permisit sibi sua auferri, ut ejus perfectio omnibus fieret nota ad ædificationem ipsorum, quemadmodum scriptum est in Tobia: Hanc autem tentationem ideo permisit Dominus evenire illi, id est Tobiæ, ut posteris daretur exemplum patientiæ ejus, sicut et sancti Job. De quo pulchre scribit Gregorius: Scriptura sacra oculis mentis quasi speculum quoddam opponitur, ut interna nostra facies in ipsa videatur. Ibi etenim fœda, ibi pulchra nostra cognoscimus. Ibi sentimus quantum proficimus; ibi videmus a profectu quam longe distamus. Narrat gesta fortium, et ad imitationem corda provocat infirmorum; dumque illorum victoriosa facta commemorat, contra vitiorum prælia nostram debilitatem confirmat, fitque verbis illius, ut eo minus mens inter certamina trepidet, quo ante se positos tot virorum fortium triumphos videt. Nonnunquam etiam quorumdam casus insinuat, ut David, quatenus timere prudenter discamus.
paras.en: Moreover, God wills the perfection of the just to be known to all; and so he willed also to show all men that holy Job's intention was just, by his patience in adversity: for which reason he permitted his goods to be taken from him, so that his perfection might become known to all for their edification, as it is written in Tobias: [[Tob 2:12|Now this trial the Lord therefore permitted to happen to him|Hanc autem tentationem ideo permisit Dominus evenire illi]], that is, to Tobias, [[Tob 2:12|that an example might be given to posterity of his patience, as also of holy Job|ut posteris daretur exemplum patientiæ ejus, sicut et sancti Job]]. Of this Gregory writes beautifully: Holy Scripture is set before the eyes of the mind like a kind of mirror, that our inward face may be seen in it. For there we come to know what is foul in us and what is fair. There we feel how far we are advancing; there we see how far we are from advancing. It tells the deeds of the strong, and stirs the hearts of the weak to imitation; and while it recounts their victorious deeds, it strengthens our weakness against the battles of the vices; and its words bring it about that the mind trembles the less amid its conflicts, the more it sees the triumphs of so many brave men set before it. Sometimes too it makes known the falls of some, as of David[[2 Kings 11:1||]] [the margin gives II Reg. xi, without a verse: David's sin with Bethsabee], so that we may learn to fear prudently.

paras.t: Egressusque est Satan a facie Domini. Quo potuit Satan exire a facie ejus qui ubique est? qui ait per Jeremiam, Cœlum et terram ego impleo. Ad quem David psalmista: Quo ibo a spiritu tuo? et quo a facie tua fugiam? Si ascendero in cœlum, tu illic es; si descendero in infernum, ades. Et respondendum, quod sicut ad Deum non acceditur passibus pedum spatiisque locorum, sed intentione sancta, affectione justisque actibus; ita ab eo receditur non corporis gressu, sed perverso affectu impioque effectu: non quod per hæc desinat intellectualis creatura esse in Dei præsentia, sed quia desinit esse coram eo, quomodo ante fuit, vel quomodo esse deberet. Egressus est itaque Satan a facie Domini, id est, per impietatis exsecutionem ab ejus supersancta voluntate per discordiam abiit: quia quod Deus bona intentione fieri licentiavit, ille perverso exsecutus est fine. Unde Albertus hic ait: Facies Domini hoc loco vocatur præsentia divinæ potestatis, iniquam diaboli voluntatem prementis, id est ab optato malitiæ actu impedientis. Sicque egressus est Satan ab obligatione seu coarctatione potestatis illius, ut non impeditus posset exercere suæ malitiam voluntatis. Juxta quem sensum intelligi potest illud Jeremiæ: Ejice illos a facie mea, et egrediantur, videlicet a defensione meæ potestatis ad licentiam seu permissionem impiæ voluntatis.
paras.en: [[1:12|And Satan went forth from the presence of the Lord|Egressusque est Satan a facie Domini]] [in Latin, *from the face of the Lord*, which the Douay-Rheims renders *from the presence*]. Whither could Satan go out from the face of him who is everywhere? who says by Jeremias, [[Jer 23:24|I fill heaven and earth|Cœlum et terram ego impleo]]; to whom David the psalmist says: [[Ps 138:7|Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy face?|Quo ibo a spiritu tuo? et quo a facie tua fugiam?]] [[Ps 138:8|If I ascend into heaven, thou art there: if I descend into hell, thou art present.|Si ascendero in cœlum, tu illic es; si descendero in infernum, ades]] It is to be answered that, as God is not approached by steps of the feet and distances of place, but by holy intention, affection and just deeds, so he is departed from not by the body's going but by perverse affection and impious deed: not that by these the intellectual creature ceases to be in God's presence, but because it ceases to be before him as it was before, or as it ought to be. [[1:12|Satan went forth from the presence of the Lord|Egressus est itaque Satan a facie Domini]], then, that is, by carrying out his impiety he went away in discord from God's most holy will: because what God allowed to be done with a good intention, he carried out with a perverse end. Hence Albert says here: The face of the Lord in this place is the name for the presence of the divine power pressing down the devil's wicked will, that is, hindering it from the act of malice it longs for. And so Satan went out from the binding or restraint of that power, so that, unhindered, he might exercise the malice of his will. In this sense can be understood that saying of Jeremias: [[Jer 15:1|cast them out from my sight, and let them go forth|Ejice illos a facie mea, et egrediantur]], namely, from the defence of my power to the licence or permission of their impious will.

paras.t: Hinc ait Gregorius: Quo exitur ab eo, qui dum per molem corporis nusquam est, per incircumscriptam substantiam nusquam deest? Sed quamdiu Satan pressus majestatis præsentia, appetitum suæ malitiæ exercere non valuit, quasi ante faciem Domini stetit; a facie Domini exiit, quia relaxatus divinitus ab internæ coarctationis angustia, ad sui effectum desiderii venit. Insuper Thomas signanter inquit: Dicitur, Egressus est a facie Domini. Satan enim secundum quod potestas nocendi ei permittitur, coram facie Domini est, quia ex rationabili voluntate hoc accidit; sed dum permissam sibi potestatem exsequitur, a facie Domini exit, quoniam ab intentione permittentis recessit. Circa hunc locum divinus et sanctus Gregorius de infinitate Dei sublimis et benedicti scribit pulcherrime, dicens: Deus manet inter omnia, ipse extra omnia, ipse supra omnia, ipse infra omnia: et superior est per potentiam, et inferior per sustentationem; et exterior per magnitudinem, et interior per subtilitatem: sursum regens, deorsum continens; extra circumdans, interius penetrans. Nec alia ex parte superior, alia inferior, atque ex alia parte exterior, et ex alia manet interior; sed unus idemque totus, ubique præsidendo sustinens, sustinendo præsidens, circumdando penetrans, penetrando circumdans. Unde superius præsidens, inde inferius sustinens, et unde exterius ambiens, inde interius replens; sine inquietudine superius regens, sine labore inferius sustinens; interius sine extenuatione penetrans, exterius sine extensione circumdans; inferior atque superior sine loco, amplus sine latitudine, subtilis sine extenuatione.
paras.en: Hence Gregory says: Whither does one go out from him who, while he is nowhere by bulk of body, is nowhere absent by his uncircumscribed substance? But so long as Satan, held down by the presence of the Majesty, could not exercise the craving of his malice, he stood as it were before the face of the Lord; he went out from the face of the Lord because, released by God from the narrow bounds of the inward restraint, he came to the effect of his desire. Moreover Thomas says pointedly: It is said, [[1:12|went forth from the presence of the Lord|Egressus est a facie Domini]]. For Satan, in so far as the power of harming is permitted him, is before the face of the Lord, because this comes about by a reasonable will; but when he carries out the power permitted him, he goes out from the face of the Lord, since he has departed from the intention of him who permits. On this place the divine and holy Gregory writes most beautifully of the infinity of God, sublime and blessed, saying: God abides within all things, himself without all things, himself above all things, himself beneath all things: and he is higher by his power, and lower by his sustaining; outer by his greatness, and inner by his subtlety: ruling above, holding together below; encompassing without, penetrating within. Nor is he higher in one part and lower in another, or outer in one part and abiding inner in another; but one and the same, wholly everywhere, sustaining by presiding, presiding by sustaining, penetrating by encompassing, encompassing by penetrating. Whence he presides above, thence he sustains below; and whence he encompasses without, thence he fills within; ruling above without disquiet, sustaining below without toil; penetrating within without being made thin, encompassing without without being stretched; lower and higher without place, ample without breadth, subtle without thinness.

paras.t: Quum autem quadam die filii et filiæ ejus comederent, et biberent vinum: quod additur, ad innuendum quod hilariter simul edebant, ut ex hoc sequens mœror appareat gravior, quia opposita juxta se posita, clarius patent, et vicissim gravius torquent. Unde in Ecclesiastico habetur: Vinum in jucunditate creatum est, non in ebrietate. In domo fratris sui primogeniti, ubi fortasse solennior convivatio fuit (et quod ait, sui, non refertur ad ejus, puta ad Job, sed ad id quod prædixit, Filii et filiæ ejus): id est in domo fratris eorum qui fuit sancti Job primogenitus, ubi forte edebant statim post egressum Satan a facie Dei. Satan enim invidiosissimus, non diu distulit implere pravum conceptum, præsertim quum secundum divinum Dionysium, in dæmonibus sit phantasia proterva, amens furor, et irrationabilis concupiscentia: amens autem furor non differt.
paras.en: [[1:13|Now upon a certain day, when his sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine|Quum autem quadam die filii et filiæ ejus comederent, et biberent vinum]]: this is added to hint that they were eating together merrily, so that the grief which follows may appear the heavier; for opposites set side by side show the more clearly, and in turn torment the more. Hence it is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 31:35|Wine was created from the beginning to make men joyful, and not to make them drunk|Vinum in jucunditate creatum est, non in ebrietate]]. Then, [[1:13|in the house of their eldest brother|In domo fratris sui primogeniti]], where perhaps the feast was kept more solemnly (and the word *sui* [“of his own”; here the Douay-Rheims has “their”] does not refer to *ejus* [“his”], that is, to Job, but to what he said before, [[1:13|his sons and daughters|Filii et filiæ ejus]]): that is, in the house of their brother, who was holy Job's firstborn; where perhaps they were eating straight after Satan went out from the face of God. For Satan, most envious, did not long put off carrying out his wicked design, especially since, according to the divine Dionysius, there is in the demons a wanton imagination, a mindless fury and an irrational concupiscence; and mindless fury does not delay.

paras.t: Nuntius venit ad Job, qui diceret: Boves arabant, et asinæ pascebantur juxta eos; et irruerunt Sabæi: qui nominantur in Joele, quo habetur, Venundabunt eos Sabæis genti longinquæ. Tuleruntque omnia pecora, ut nec victui nec agriculturæ necessaria remanerent ex illis; et pueros, id est pecorum custodes et servos Job, percusserunt, id est occiderunt, gladio. Ex quo sequitur, quod non solum sobolem, sed et familiam Job Deus tradiderit manui Satanæ, quantum ad corporalem tribulationem. Et evasi ego solus, ut nuntiarem tibi, improvise ac subito ad majorem tui afflictionem, quia jacula prævisa minus feriunt. Ideoque Satan unum abire permisit ac fugere, ut per importunam ac turbulentam ejus denuntiationem, Job amplius moveretur et turbaretur: qui etiam tanquam vir justus magis de puerorum occisione, quam pecorum ablatione dolebat. Istud in die convivii accidit, quia secundum Gregorium, prænuntia tribulationis est lætitia satietatis. Unde et scriptum est: Risus dolore miscebitur, et extrema gaudii luctus occupat. Sed et frequenter rota fortunæ quem ad summa elevat prius, ad ima declinat, et vice versa.
paras.en: [[1:14|There came a messenger to Job, and said|Nuntius venit ad Job, qui diceret]]: [[1:14|The oxen were ploughing, and the asses feeding beside them|Boves arabant, et asinæ pascebantur juxta eos]]; [[1:15|And the Sabeans rushed in|et irruerunt Sabæi]], who are named in Joel, where it says: [[Joel 3:8|they shall sell them to the Sabeans, a nation far off|Venundabunt eos Sabæis genti longinquæ]]. [[1:15|and took all away|Tuleruntque omnia]]: all the beasts, so that none of them was left that was needed either for food or for tilling; and [[1:15|the servants|et pueros]] (that is, the keepers of the beasts and Job's household servants) they [[1:15|slew|percusserunt]], that is, killed, [[1:15|with the sword|gladio]]. From this it follows that God delivered into Satan's hand not only Job's offspring but also his household, as far as bodily tribulation goes. [[1:15|and I alone have escaped to tell thee|Et evasi ego solus, ut nuntiarem tibi]], unforeseen and suddenly, to thy greater affliction, for darts foreseen strike less. And so Satan let one go off and flee, so that by his untimely and agitated announcement Job might be the more moved and troubled; who also, as a just man, grieved more over the slaying of the servants than over the taking of the beasts. This happened on a day of feasting because, according to Gregory, the gladness of fullness is the forerunner of tribulation. Hence it is written: [[Prov 14:13|Laughter shall be mingled with sorrow, and mourning taketh hold of the ends of joy|Risus dolore miscebitur, et extrema gaudii luctus occupat]]. And often, too, the wheel of fortune first lifts a man to the heights and then brings him down to the depths, and the other way round.

paras.t: Quumque adhuc ille loqueretur, venit alter, unus scilicet puerorum oves custodientium, ut videtur, et dixit: Ignis Dei, id est divinitus permissus, vel secundum æstimationem loquentis, a Deo pro plaga inductus et supernaturaliter procuratus, cecidit de cælo aereo, et tactas oves puerosque consumpsit, id est, repente dum tetigit oves tuas et earum pastores, simul cuncta consumpsit: cum tanto impetu furoreque venit. Et effugi ego solus, ut nuntiarem tibi. Ideo Satan practicavit, quod unus ita effugeret ac subito ad Job veniret, altero adhuc loquente, quatenus adversitas adversitati adjuncta, et sine intervallo percepta, mentem sancti Job magis obrueret, dum se per temporis interpolationem ad patientiam non armaret. Denique, quod dicitur, Ignis Dei, quidam exponunt, Ignis Dei, id est missus a Deo: quod non videtur congrue dictum, quoniam ignem istum Satan produxit in aere, fecitque descendere. Deus autem nec per se ipsum, nec per angelum bonum, sed per Satan afflixit Job, ita quod dæmon ignem hunc procuravit: quod naturali industria et virtute faciliter potuit, activa atque passiva materialia invicem applicando. Unde et in Apocalypsi legitur: Bestia, id est Antichristus seu ejus caterva, fecit signa magna, ut etiam ignem faceret de cælo descendere in conspectu hominum: quod (secundum expositores ibidem) fiet operatione diaboli. Aliqui etiam dicunt, quod ignis iste cecidit de cælo per coruscationem et fulgur. Sed magis opinor, quod directe ex aere irruit, nec per terræ gyrum, sed per locum dumtaxat ubi oves et pastores fuerant, fundebatur et extendebatur. Dicitur tamen ignis Dei, quia permissus a Deo, vel ob aliam causam prætactam. Hinc dicit Gregorius: Intuendum quam callide dicitur, Ignis Dei, ac si diceretur, Illius iram sustines, cui quotidie sic servisti totque hostias obtulisti, ut Job de exhibito Deo obsequio tristaretur, seque ei frustra servisse conquereretur.
paras.en: [[1:16|And while he was yet speaking, another came|Quumque adhuc ille loqueretur, venit alter]], that is, one of the servants who kept the sheep, it would seem, [[1:16|and said|et dixit]]: [[1:16|The fire of God|Ignis Dei]], that is, permitted by God; or, as the speaker reckoned it, brought by God as a scourge and procured supernaturally, [[1:16|fell from heaven|cecidit de cælo]] (the heaven of the air), [[1:16|and striking the sheep and the servants, hath consumed them|et tactas oves puerosque consumpsit]]: that is, as soon as it touched thy sheep and their shepherds, it consumed them all at once, with such force and fury did it come. [[1:16|and I alone have escaped to tell thee|Et effugi ego solus, ut nuntiarem tibi]]. Satan contrived it so that one should escape in this way and come suddenly to Job while the other was still speaking, so that adversity joined to adversity, and taken in without a pause, might the more overwhelm holy Job's mind, since he could not arm himself to patience in an interval of time. Further, as to the words *The fire of God*, some explain: *the fire of God*, that is, sent by God. This does not seem fitly said, since Satan produced this fire in the air and made it come down. For God afflicted Job neither by himself nor by a good angel, but by Satan, so that it was the demon who procured this fire: which by his natural skill and power he could easily do, by applying active and passive materials to one another. Hence we read in the Apocalypse also: The beast, that is, Antichrist or his band, [[Apoc 13:13|did great signs, so that he made also fire to come down from heaven unto the earth, in the sight of men|fecit signa magna, ut etiam ignem faceret de cælo descendere in conspectu hominum]]; which (according to the commentators on that place) will come about by the working of the devil. Some also say that this fire fell from heaven by way of lightning and thunderbolt. But I rather think that it rushed straight down out of the air, and poured out and spread not over the round of the earth but only over the place where the sheep and shepherds had been. Yet it is called *the fire of God* because it was permitted by God, or for the other reason touched on above. Hence Gregory says: Note how cunningly it is said, *The fire of God*, as if to say: Thou bearest the wrath of him whom thou hast served so daily, and to whom thou hast offered so many victims; so that Job might grieve over the service he had shown to God, and complain that he had served him in vain.

paras.t: Sed et illo adhuc loquente, venit alius puer custosque pecorum, et dixit: Chaldæi: de quorum maxima crudelitate in Jeremia, Joele et Habacuc multa dicuntur; fecerunt tres turmas, cingentes quæ tua fuerunt, ne quidquam tuorum evaderet; et invaserunt camelos, et tulerunt eos, et pueros percusserunt gladio; et effugi ego solus, ut nuntiarem tibi, addendo dolorem dolori.
paras.en: [[1:17|And while he also was yet speaking, there came another|Sed et illo adhuc loquente, venit alius]], a servant and keeper of the beasts, [[1:17|and said|et dixit]]: [[1:17|The Chaldeans|Chaldæi]], of whose very great cruelty much is said in Jeremias[[Jer 6:23||]], Joel[[Joel 2:3||]] and Habacuc[[Hab 1:6||]] [the margin here is only partly legible: it seems to cite Jer. vi, 22–23, Joel i, 6–7 and ii, 3–6, and Habac. i, 6; the verse numbers are uncertain], [[1:17|made three troops|fecerunt tres turmas]], surrounding all that was thine, so that nothing of thine should escape; [[1:17|and have fallen upon the camels, and taken them|et invaserunt camelos, et tulerunt eos]]; [[1:17|moreover, they have slain the servants with the sword|et pueros percusserunt gladio]]: [[1:17|and I alone have escaped to tell thee|et effugi ego solus, ut nuntiarem tibi]], adding sorrow to sorrow.

paras.t: Pensandum, quod quatuor tribulationes denuntiantur beato Job: quas Satan sic ordinavit, quod duæ ab hominibus inferrentur, duæ divinitus crederentur illatæ; et prima ab hominibus illata ipsi Job nuntiata, nuntiaretur secunda desuper facta, deinde tertia ab hominibus inflicta, et ultimo quarta desuper lapsa: quod hostis antiquus callidissime ad doloris procuravit augmentum. Mens nempe justorum, ab hominibus sumpta injuria, consolationem in Deo requirit: quem si mox viderit sibi adversa exaggerare et plagas augere, magis affligitur.
paras.en: It is to be weighed that four tribulations are announced to blessed Job, which Satan so arranged that two were inflicted by men and two were believed to have been brought on by God; and that when the first, inflicted by men, had been announced to Job, the second should be announced, coming from above, then the third, inflicted by men, and last the fourth, falling from above: which the old enemy most cunningly contrived for the increase of his sorrow. For the mind of the just, when it has suffered injury from men, seeks consolation in God; and if it soon sees him heaping up adversities upon it and increasing its stripes, it is the more afflicted.

paras.t: Adhuc loquebatur ille, et ecce alius intravit, et dixit: Filiis tuis et filiabus vescentibus et bibentibus vinum in domo fratris sui primogeniti, repente ventus vehemens irruit a regione deserti, et concussit quatuor angulos domus: quæ corruens, oppressit liberos tuos: nec dubium quin et filias, quæ ad fugiendum fuerant tardiores; et mortui sunt, et effugi ego solus, ut nuntiarem tibi. Unde videtur quod omnes qui erant in domo, oppressi sint, isto excepto, qui forte vento irruente fuit in janua aut extra domum: estque verisimile, quod multi cum filiis et filiabus Job fuerunt in domo, præsertim de ministrantibus ad mensam filiis ac filiabus tam inclyti principis: et forte si filii Job vel saltem primogenitus ejus habuit sobolem, simul exstincta est. Hæc autem adversitas præcedentibus tanto molestior fuit, quo filii plus diliguntur quam servi et facultates: et quia omnes filii et filiæ simul exstincti sunt, ita quod spes posteritatis non mansit; et rursus, quia in tali opere in quo periculosum est mori, fuerunt consumpti, videlicet in convivio, in quo peccata deesse non solent; quod item tam improvise ac subito, ita quod se ad mortem per pœnitentiam disponere aut non, aut vix valebant. Ex quibus omnibus generabatur timorato patri sollicitudo et timor de aliquo forte periculo animarum eorum, præsertim quoad venialia non minima: nam et ante, tempore convivii, misit ad eos, sanctificavitque ipsos, timens quod Deum offenderint. Præterea innuendum quam hostiliter et astute dæmon invasit Job. Primo enim induxit nocumenta minora, deinde majora, ut unumquodque per se gravius atque distinctius sentiretur: nam nocumenta ac damna minora post majora statim illata, parum aut nil sentiuntur. Quemadmodum enim parvum lumen cum magno non percipitur, sed fuscatur, sic minus tristabile, non sentitur immediate post majus.
paras.en: [[1:18|He was yet speaking, and behold another came in|Adhuc loquebatur ille, et ecce alius intravit]], [[1:18|and said|et dixit]]: [[1:18|Thy sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their eldest brother|Filiis tuis et filiabus vescentibus et bibentibus vinum in domo fratris sui primogeniti]], [[1:19|A violent wind came on a sudden from the side of the desert, and shook the four corners of the house, and it fell upon thy children|repente ventus vehemens irruit a regione deserti, et concussit quatuor angulos domus: quæ corruens, oppressit liberos tuos]] (and no doubt the daughters too, who had been slower to flee), [[1:19|and they are dead: and I alone have escaped to tell thee|et mortui sunt, et effugi ego solus, ut nuntiarem tibi]]. Hence it seems that all who were in the house were crushed, save this one, who perhaps was at the door or outside the house when the wind rushed in. And it is likely that many were in the house with Job's sons and daughters, especially of those who served at table the sons and daughters of so renowned a prince; and if Job's sons, or at least his firstborn, had offspring, perhaps it was wiped out with them. Now this adversity was the more grievous than those before it, inasmuch as children are loved more than servants and goods; and because all the sons and daughters were wiped out together, so that no hope of posterity remained; and again, because they were carried off in such an occupation as it is perilous to die in, namely at a feast, where sins are not usually lacking; and also so unforeseen and suddenly that they were able to dispose themselves for death by penance either not at all or barely. From all these things there arose in the God-fearing father anxiety and fear of some danger, perhaps, to their souls, especially as regards venial sins, and those not of the least: for before, too, at the time of the feast, he had sent to them and sanctified them, fearing that they had offended God[[1:5||]]. It should be pointed out besides how hostilely and astutely the demon attacked Job. For first he brought on the lesser harms, then the greater, so that each might be felt the more heavily and distinctly by itself: for lesser harms and losses inflicted straight after greater ones are felt little or not at all. For just as a small light is not perceived beside a great one, but is darkened, so what saddens less is not felt immediately after what saddens more.

paras.t: Circa hæc scribit Thomas: Quum omnis adversitas prædicta sit per Satan inducta, necesse est confiteri, quod Deo permittente dæmones possint aeris perturbationes inducere, ventos concitare, ignem e cælo dejicere. Quamvis enim natura corporalis non obediat angelis bonis nec malis, quantum ad substantialium susceptionem formarum, sed soli Deo, obedit tamen eis quoad motum localem: cujus signum est, quod in homine ex solo voluntatis imperio membra ad opus moventur. Quæcumque ergo solo motu locali fieri possunt, hæc per naturalem virtutem angeli boni ac mali facere possunt, nisi divinitus prohibeantur. Venti autem et pluvia et aliæ hujusmodi aeris perturbationes solo motu vaporum resolutorum ex terra et aqua fieri possunt. Nec obviat illud Jeremiæ: Numquid sunt in sculptilibus gentium qui pluant? Aliud enim est naturali cursu pluere, quod solius est Dei, qui causas naturales ad hoc ordinavit; aliud, causis naturalibus a Deo ad pluendum ordinatis aliquando artificialiter uti, ad pluviam vel ventum interdum quasi extraordinarie producendum.
paras.en: On these things Thomas writes: Since all the adversity described was brought on by Satan, we must confess that, with God's permission, demons can bring about disturbances of the air, stir up winds and cast fire down from heaven. For although bodily nature does not obey the angels, good or bad, as regards the receiving of substantial forms [that is, the forms that make a thing the kind of thing it is, as distinct from its accidents], but obeys God alone, it does obey them as regards local motion: a sign of which is that in man the members are moved to their work by the mere command of the will. Whatever things, then, can be done by local motion alone, these the angels, good and bad, can do by their natural power, unless God prevents them. Now winds and rain and other such disturbances of the air can be brought about by the mere motion of vapours released from earth and water. Nor does that saying of Jeremias stand in the way: [[Jer 14:22|Are there any among the graven things of the Gentiles that can send rain?|Numquid sunt in sculptilibus gentium qui pluant?]] For it is one thing to make rain by the course of nature, which belongs to God alone, who ordained natural causes for this; another to make use at times, by art, of the natural causes ordained by God for making rain, so as now and then to produce rain or wind in a way somewhat out of the ordinary.

paras.t: Insuper ait Gregorius: Notandum, quam callide tot malorum pondera, et divisa et subita nuntiantur, ut et repente et particulatim crescens in audientis corde, sese dolor ipse non caperet; et tanto ardentius in blasphemiam accenderet, quanto subitis ac multiplicibus nuntiis in se angustius æstuaret. Postremo Gregorius sentit filios et filias sancti Job virtuose vixisse, sobrie refecisse, salubriterque obiisse: Absit, inquiens, ne tanti viri filios per conviviorum studia ingurgitando ventri suspicemur vacasse.
paras.en: Gregory says further: Note how cunningly the weight of so many evils is announced, both piecemeal and suddenly, so that sorrow, growing in the hearer's heart both all at once and bit by bit, might not be able to contain itself, and might kindle into blasphemy the more fiercely, the more narrowly it seethed within him under the sudden and many messages. Lastly, Gregory holds that holy Job's sons and daughters lived virtuously, took their meals soberly, and died in a state of salvation. Far be it from us, he says, to suspect that the sons of so great a man gave themselves up, in their zeal for feasting, to gorging the belly.

paras.t: Tunc, videlicet morte totius sobolis suæ audita, surrexit Job, non pusillanimitate dejectus, sed in Deum mente erectus, et scidit vestimenta sua, et tonso capite, corruens in terram, adoravit. Apud antiquos signum tristitiæ fuit utrumque istorum, videlicet scindere vestes, atque abradere crines. Nec mirum si Job tot filiis ac filiabus amissis hæc fecerit, quum in Genesi scriptum sit, quemadmodum patriarcha Jacob putans Joseph a bestia devoratum, scissis vestibus, indutus sit cilicio, lugens filium tempore multo. Denique ex hoc quod Job primo surrexit, deinde vestes scidit, et caput totondit, atque deinceps in terram corruit, Deumque adoravit, ostenditur quod non ex mentis immoderato mœrore, sed ex vera devotione solo tenus se prostravit.
paras.en: [[1:20|Then|Tunc]], that is, when he had heard of the death of all his offspring, [[1:20|Job rose up|surrexit Job]], not cast down by faintheartedness but lifted up in mind to God, [[1:20|and rent his garments, and having shaven his head|et scidit vestimenta sua, et tonso capite]], [[1:20|fell down upon the ground, and worshipped|corruens in terram, adoravit]]. Among the ancients each of these was a sign of sorrow, namely to rend one's garments and to shave off one's hair. Nor is it any wonder that Job did these things when he had lost so many sons and daughters, since it is written in Genesis how the patriarch Jacob, thinking that Joseph had been devoured by a beast[[Gen 37:33||]], mourned: [[Gen 37:34|tearing his garments, he put on sackcloth, mourning for his son a long time|scissis vestibus, indutus sit cilicio, lugens filium tempore multo]]. Lastly, from the fact that Job first rose up, then rent his garments and cut off his hair, and after that fell down upon the ground and worshipped God, it is shown that he prostrated himself to the ground not out of immoderate grief of mind but out of true devotion.

paras.t: Sed quum Salomon dicat, Non contristabit justum quidquid ei acciderit, quomodo Job signifer æquitatis, in adversis tristatus est, præsertim quum perfectæ patientiæ sit, etiam cum delectatione sustinere adversa? Et respondendum, quod verbum Salomonis de inordinata, sæculari et irrefrenata tristitia accipi debet, quæ animum obruit, rationem excæcat, et juxta Apostolum, efficit mortem: de qua in Ecclesiastico dicitur, Tristitiam non des animæ tuæ, et non affligas te ipsum in consilio tuo. Moderata vero tristitia non est abjicienda: de qua in Ecclesiaste fertur, Cor sapientium ubi tristitia; cor stultorum ubi lætitia. Sed et de Christo Evangelista testatur quod dixit, Tristis est anima mea usque ad mortem. Imo quod Salomon ait, Non contristabit justum quidquid ei acciderit, de malo culpæ intelligi nequit, nisi quoad immoderantiam quamdam tristitiæ, præsertim quum de Christo in Marco scriptum sit: Contristatus est super cæcitate cordis eorum.
paras.en: But since Solomon says, [[Prov 12:21|Whatsoever shall befall the just man, shall not make him sad|Non contristabit justum quidquid ei acciderit]], how was Job, the standard-bearer of justice, saddened in adversity, especially since it belongs to perfect patience to bear adversities even with delight? The answer is that Solomon's saying must be taken of disordered, worldly and unbridled sadness, which overwhelms the mind, blinds the reason and, according to the Apostle, [[2 Cor 7:10|worketh death|efficit mortem]]; of which it is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 30:22|Give not up thy soul to sadness, and afflict not thyself in thy own counsel|Tristitiam non des animæ tuæ, et non affligas te ipsum in consilio tuo]]. But moderate sadness is not to be cast off; of which it is said in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 7:5|The heart of the wise is where there is mourning, and the heart of fools where there is mirth|Cor sapientium ubi tristitia; cor stultorum ubi lætitia]]. And the Evangelist bears witness of Christ, too, that he said: [[Matt 26:38|My soul is sorrowful even unto death|Tristis est anima mea usque ad mortem]]. Indeed, what Solomon says, [[Prov 12:21|Whatsoever shall befall the just man, shall not make him sad|Non contristabit justum quidquid ei acciderit]], cannot be understood of sadness over the evil of guilt [that is, the evil of sin, as distinct from the evil of punishment] except as regards a certain immoderation of sadness; especially since it is written of Christ in Mark: [[Mark 3:5|being grieved for the blindness of their hearts|Contristatus est super cæcitate cordis eorum]].

paras.t: Porro quomodo timor et tristitia ac ceteræ passiones cadant in virum constantem, seu virtuoso sint assumendæ, B. Augustinus in libris de Civitate Dei prolixe pertractat, recitans diversas de hoc philosophorum opiniones. Stoici enim dicebant, quod nullo modo cadunt in virum constantem et sapientem. Peripatetici vero dicebant, quod passiones de se non sunt virtuosæ aut vitiosæ, sed naturales quædam affectiones et motus: ideo secundum rationis dictamen possunt sine culpa inesse atque assumi cum moderamine, ita quod rationem non obruant: hancque sententiam fassus est Augustinus sacræ Scripturæ consonantiorem esse ac veram. Idem quoque hoc loco affirmat Gregorius. Augustinus insuper, super illud Apostoli ad Thessalonicenses, Nolumus vos ignorare de dormientibus, ut non contristemini sicut et ceteri qui spem non habent, dicit in quodam sermone: Non prohibet Apostolus de morte carorum ac propinquorum tristari; sed prohibet sic tristari sicut infideles tristantur, spe resurrectionis carentes, sicque dolentes quasi defuncti omnino esse desierint. Et iterum ait: Non possumus caris ac propinquis defunctis penitus non tristari. Præterea Stoici asserebant, bona exteriora nullo modo esse hominis bona, ideo de eorum amissione nullo modo esse dolendum: cujus opinionis fuit et Craton philosophus, antequam a Joanne apostolo converteretur, prout in beatissimi Joannis continetur Legenda. Peripatetici vero dicebant bona exteriora esse hominis bona minus principalia ac instrumentalia ad virtutes, sicut et corpus ordinatur ad animam: ideo de eorum amissione moderanter posse tristari, quando videlicet homo sic eis privatur, quod juxta sui exigentiam status non retinet competentiam.
paras.en: Further, how fear and sadness and the other passions befall a steadfast man, or how a virtuous man is to take them on, blessed Augustine treats at length in the books of the City of God, recounting the different opinions of the philosophers on this. For the Stoics said that they in no way befall a steadfast and wise man. But the Peripatetics said that the passions are not of themselves virtuous or vicious, but are certain natural affections and movements: and so, following the dictate of reason, they can be present without fault and be taken on with moderation, so that they do not overwhelm the reason. And this opinion Augustine declared to be more in harmony with Holy Scripture, and true. Gregory too affirms the same in this place. Augustine, moreover, on that saying of the Apostle to the Thessalonians, [[1 Thess 4:12|we will not have you ignorant brethren, concerning them that are asleep, that you be not sorrowful, even as others who have no hope|Nolumus vos ignorare de dormientibus, ut non contristemini sicut et ceteri qui spem non habent]], says in a certain sermon: The Apostle does not forbid us to be sad at the death of those dear and near to us; but he forbids us to be sad as unbelievers are sad, who lack the hope of the resurrection, and so grieve as though the dead had altogether ceased to be. And again he says: We cannot be wholly without sadness when those dear and near to us have died. Further, the Stoics asserted that external goods are in no way goods of man, and that their loss is therefore in no way to be grieved over: of which opinion was also the philosopher Craton, before he was converted by John the apostle, as is contained in the Legend of the most blessed John [in the story, Craton had two rich young men break up their jewels in contempt of riches]. But the Peripatetics said that external goods are goods of man, though less principal ones, and instruments for the virtues, just as the body too is ordered to the soul: and so one may be moderately saddened by their loss, namely when a man is so deprived of them that he does not keep what is fitting for the needs of his state.

paras.t: Sicque Job in contristando se habuit: quem etiam arbitror Deum adorando orasse pro suis defunctis, et ne laberetur ipse in aliquam culpam. Et quoniam, sicut paulo post subditur, gratias egit Deo, constat quod secundum rationis suæ supremum, aliquo modo gavisus sit in præfatis adversis, considerando ea ut secundum Dei beneplacitum sibi inflicta, et ut materia magni meriti exstiterunt. Gaudium nempe est diffusio animi in conceptu boni.
paras.en: And so Job bore himself in his sadness; and I think too that in worshipping God he prayed for his dead, and that he himself might not fall into any fault. And since, as is added a little after, he gave thanks to God, it is plain that in the highest part of his reason he in some way rejoiced in the adversities just mentioned, considering them as inflicted on him according to God's good pleasure, and as having been matter of great merit. For joy is the expansion of the mind in the conceiving of a good.

paras.t: Et dixit: Nudus egressus sum de utero matris meæ: quod de propriæ genitricis utero accipi posset, nisi mox adderet, et nudus revertar illuc. Itaque, per uterum matris suæ, intellexit uterum terræ, quæ omnium mortalium communis est mater: cujus uterus est aliquod receptaculum ejus, in quod redit homo per sepulturam ac corporis resolutionem, juxta quod dictum est Adæ: In sudore vultus tui vesceris pane tuo, donec revertaris in terram de qua sumptus es, quia pulvis es, et in pulverem reverteris. Sed quum defunctorum corpora soleant aliquo operimento tecta sepeliri, quomodo Job rediit nudus in terram, quem constat cum maxima solennitate et forte pretiosis opertum in monumento locatum? Et respondendum, quod per nuditatem signatur carentia opum ac rerum, quantum ad possessionem; certum est autem, quod corpus exanime nihil possideat. Porro, quod terra mater hominum appelletur, patet ex Ecclesiastico in quo habetur: Occupatio magna creata est omnibus hominibus, et jugum grave super omnes filios Adam, a die exitus de ventre matris eorum, usque in diem sepulturæ in matrem omnium. Præhabito quoque Job verbo consonat illud Apostoli ad Timotheum: Nihil intulimus in hunc mundum; haud dubium quia nec auferre quid possumus. Verumtamen videtur verbum inductum, de ventre matris carnalis posse exponi: et quod ait, Nudus revertar illuc, intelligendum erit non de ventre hujusmodi matris, sed de aliquo ei proportionabili aut simili, puta de monumento, in quo corpus post egressum de mundo latet atque quiescit, sicut ante ingressum in mundum in utero matris latuit et quievit. Quibus verbis sanctus Job ex consideratione conditionis suæ mortalis naturæ rationabiliter demonstravit quod de rerum amissione non debuit tristitia absorberi, vinci aut dejici, quum rerum possessio accidentalis, non substantialis sit homini. Itaque magna in rerum amissione est consolatio, sapienter pensare quod aliquando nihil earum habuimus, et tandem nihil de eis habebimus. Consequenter idem demonstrat ex parte Dei, qui omnia dedit, et cujus beneplacito homo conformare se debet.
paras.en: [[1:21|And said|Et dixit]]: [[1:21|Naked came I out of my mother's womb|Nudus egressus sum de utero matris meæ]]: which might be taken of the womb of his own mother, were he not to add at once, [[1:21|and naked shall I return thither|et nudus revertar illuc]]. So by the womb of his mother he understood the womb of the earth, which is the common mother of all mortals: whose womb is a kind of receptacle of hers, into which man returns by burial and the dissolving of the body, according to what was said to Adam: [[Gen 3:19|In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread till thou return to the earth out of which thou wast taken: for dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return|In sudore vultus tui vesceris pane tuo, donec revertaris in terram de qua sumptus es, quia pulvis es, et in pulverem reverteris]]. But since the bodies of the dead are usually buried covered with some wrapping, how did Job return naked into the earth, when it is certain that he was laid in the tomb with the greatest solemnity, and perhaps covered with precious things? The answer is that by nakedness is signified the lack of wealth and things as regards possession; and it is certain that a lifeless body possesses nothing. Further, that the earth is called the mother of men is plain from Ecclesiasticus, where it says: [[Ecclus 40:1|Great labour is created for all men, and a heavy yoke is upon the children of Adam from the day of their coming out of their mother's womb, until the day of their burial into the mother of all|Occupatio magna creata est omnibus hominibus, et jugum grave super omnes filios Adam, a die exitus de ventre matris eorum, usque in diem sepulturæ in matrem omnium]]. With Job's saying above there agrees also that saying of the Apostle to Timothy: [[1 Tim 6:7|For we brought nothing into this world: and certainly we can carry nothing out|Nihil intulimus in hunc mundum; haud dubium quia nec auferre quid possumus]]. Yet it seems that the saying brought forward can be explained of the womb of his mother in the flesh; and then what he says, [[1:21|naked shall I return thither|Nudus revertar illuc]], will have to be understood not of the womb of such a mother, but of something proportioned or like to it, namely the tomb, in which the body after leaving the world lies hidden and rests, as before entering the world it lay hidden and rested in its mother's womb. By these words holy Job, from the consideration of the condition of his mortal nature, reasonably showed that he ought not to be swallowed up, overcome or cast down by sadness at the loss of things, since the possession of things is accidental to man, not of his substance. And so there is great consolation in the loss of things in wisely weighing that once we had none of them, and in the end we shall have nothing of them. Next he shows the same from God's side, who gave all things, and to whose good pleasure man ought to conform himself.

paras.t: Dominus dedit, qui omnium est bonorum origo, creator, collator, qui (ut Jacobus ait) dat omnibus affluenter, et non improperat. Joannes quoque Baptista protestatur: Non potest homo accipere quidquam, nisi fuerit ei datum de cælo. Per hoc autem quod ait, Dominus dedit, fassus est Job, prosperitatem mundanam opulentiamque terrenam non casualiter, neque ex fato, nec ex solo humano studio, sed ex dispensatione divina hominibus provenire. Similiter adversitates vitæ præsentis insinuans ex divinæ providentiæ fonte contingere, subdit: Dominus abstulit, id est, auferri permisit. Quamvis autem Job audivit sibi opes ablatas a Sabæis atque Chaldæis hominibus pravis, id tamen Deo adscripsit, sine cujus permissu et ordinatione scivit nec ista nec aliqua fieri. Rursus, quoniam res a Deo concessas nullus tenet, nisi conservante eo qui dedit, ablatio rerum quamvis sit a maligno directe et effective, Deo tamen adscribitur, juxta Scripturarum consuetudinem, quæ hominum indurationem, errorem, aversionem Deo attribuit, eo quod nemo nisi per misericordiam Dei ad pœnitentiam salubriter emolliatur, juste conversetur, ad Dominum convertatur. Hinc in Exodo Dominus ait frequenter: Indurabo cor Pharaonis. Et Psalmista ad Deum, Declinasti, inquit, semitas nostras a via tua. Et Isaias: Quare nos errare fecisti de viis tuis, indurasti corda nostra ne timeremus te? Itaque, quoniam Deus temporalia gratis dedit, potest ea ad placitum irreprehensibiliter tollere: ejus enim sunt omnia. Propter quod de earum perditione nec murmurare, nec conqueri, nec immoderanter debet homo tristari.
paras.en: [[1:21|the Lord gave|Dominus dedit]], who is the origin, creator and bestower of all goods, who (as James says) [[Jas 1:5|giveth to all men abundantly and upbraideth not|dat omnibus affluenter, et non improperat]]. John the Baptist too declares: [[John 3:27|A man cannot receive any thing, unless it be given him from heaven|Non potest homo accipere quidquam, nisi fuerit ei datum de cælo]]. By saying *the Lord gave*, Job confessed that worldly prosperity and earthly wealth come to men not by chance, nor from fate, nor from human effort alone, but by God's dispensation. Likewise, intimating that the adversities of the present life come from the fountain of divine providence, he adds: [[1:21|and the Lord hath taken away|Dominus abstulit]], that is, permitted it to be taken away. Now although Job heard that his wealth had been taken from him by the Sabeans and the Chaldeans, wicked men, he nevertheless ascribed it to God, without whose permission and ordinance he knew that neither these things nor any others come about. Again, since no one holds the things granted by God unless he who gave them preserves them, the taking away of things, though it is directly and effectively from the evil one, is still ascribed to God, after the custom of the Scriptures, which attribute to God men's hardening, error and turning away, because no one is softened to penance unto salvation, lives justly, or is turned to the Lord, except through God's mercy. Hence in Exodus the Lord often says[[Ex 4:21||]][[Ex 9:12||]][[Ex 10:1||]][[Ex 10:20||]][[Ex 10:27||]][[Ex 11:10||]][[Ex 14:4||]][[Ex 14:17||]]: [[Ex 7:3|I shall harden his heart|Indurabo cor Pharaonis]] [Denis has “I will harden Pharao's heart”; the margin, partly misread in the scan, seems to give Exod. iv, 21; vii, 3; ix, 12; x, 1, 20, 27; xi, 10; xiv, 4, 17, the places where the Lord says he will harden Pharao's heart or is said to have hardened it]. And the Psalmist to God: [[Ps 43:19|hast thou turned aside|Declinasti]], he says, [[Ps 43:19|our steps from thy way|semitas nostras a via tua]] [the Douay-Rheims, following the sense of the verse, reads “neither hast thou turned aside our steps”; Denis takes the words as “thou hast turned aside our steps from thy way”]. And Isaias: [[Is 63:17|Why hast thou made us to err, O Lord, from thy ways: why hast thou hardened our heart, that we should not fear thee?|Quare nos errare fecisti de viis tuis, indurasti corda nostra ne timeremus te?]] And so, since God gave temporal things freely, he can take them away at his pleasure without reproach: for all things are his. Wherefore man ought not to murmur, nor complain, nor be immoderately saddened at their loss.

paras.t: Sicut Domino placuit, ita factum est. Ideo debeo contentari, et ejus voluntati me conformare. Amicorum namque est eadem velle et nolle: idcirco diligens Deum, de ejus dispositione secundum rationem contentus est. Sed quomodo injusta spoliatio opum, atque crudelis occisio filiorum Job, placuit Deo, cui nil impium placet? Et respondendum, quod ista Deo placuerunt eo modo et fine, quo ipse ea permisit, videlicet in quantum erant ad profectum Job, atque ob utilitatem multiplicem, non in quantum processerunt ex impia voluntate dæmonis et hominum quos induxit ad vitia. Dicit autem Gregorius: Dum quæ nolumus patimur, necesse est ut ad Deum qui injustum nil vult, nostram voluntatem vertamus. Magna quippe est consolatio in eo quod displicet, quod Deo ordinante circa nos agitur, cui non nisi justum placet.
paras.en: [[1:21|as it hath pleased the Lord, so is it done|Sicut Domino placuit, ita factum est]]: therefore I ought to be content, and to conform myself to his will. For it belongs to friends to will and not to will the same things; and so one who loves God is content, according to reason, with what he disposes. But how did the unjust plundering of Job's wealth and the cruel slaughter of his children please God, whom nothing wicked pleases? The answer is that these things pleased God in the way and for the end for which he permitted them, namely inasmuch as they served Job's advancement, and for manifold profit; not inasmuch as they proceeded from the wicked will of the demon and of the men whom he led into vice. And Gregory says: When we suffer what we do not will, we must turn our will to God, who wills nothing unjust. For there is great consolation in what displeases us in this, that it is done to us by the ordering of God, whom nothing but what is just pleases.

paras.t: Sit nomen Domini nominatum benedictum, id est, ipse omnium Dominus, nomine nominante designatus, ab omnibus benedicatur, et in se ipso sanctus, bonus, omnique bona dictione et appellatione condignus esse noscatur. Sic ergo finaliter sanctus Job verba sua in Dei laude et gratiarum actione finivit, in adversis lætatus secundum quasdam sapientiales considerationes, videlicet ut erant ex beneplacito Dei, et pro gratiæ incremento, quamvis in se ipsis contristabilia essent: quemadmodum æger de pœnali medicina secundum rationem gaudet, ut est effectiva sanitatis, et longe pœnalitatis ablativa, quamvis sensus ex objecto sibi improportionato tristetur et affligatur. Quemadmodum Gregorius scribit: Sanctus Job acriora valde vulnera ipsi Satan inflixit, quam ab eo sustinuit: quot enim voces patientiæ in laude Dei percussus reddidit, quasi tot jacula in adversarii pectus intorsit. Nos quoque contra tentatorem jacula mittimus, si tribulationibus confossi, humilia respondemus.
paras.en: [[1:21|blessed be the name of the Lord|Sit nomen Domini nominatum benedictum]]: that is, may he who is Lord of all, designated by the name that names him, be blessed by all, and be known to be in himself holy, good, and worthy of every good word and title. So in the end holy Job finished his words in the praise of God and in giving thanks, rejoicing in adversity according to certain considerations of wisdom, namely inasmuch as these things came from God's good pleasure and were for the increase of grace, although in themselves they were matter for sadness: just as a sick man, according to reason, rejoices in a painful medicine inasmuch as it brings about health and drives pain far away, although the sense is saddened and afflicted by an object out of proportion to it. As Gregory writes: Holy Job inflicted far sharper wounds on Satan himself than he suffered from him; for as many words of patience as he gave back in the praise of God when he was struck, so many darts, as it were, did he hurl into the adversary's breast. We too send darts against the tempter if, pierced through with tribulations, we answer with humble words.

paras.t: In omnibus his, ejus tribulationibus et adversis, non peccavit Job labiis suis, inordinate, impatienter, murmurose loquendo: in quo patet ejus perfectio, quia, ut dicit Jacobus, Si quis in verbo non offendit, hic perfectus est vir. Neque stultum quid contra Deum locutus est, id est, nihil quod veræ sapientiæ, quæ est cognitio divinorum, contrariatur, expressit, sicut aliqui imperfecti et passionati, qui dum aliquid vident aut sustinent quod eis multum irrationabile et injustum videtur, de providentia Dei incipiunt dubitare ac indecentia verba effari. Non autem ignoravit beatus Job Deum esse tam bonum ac sapientem, quod nequaquam sineret fieri mala, nisi sciret, vellet et posset ex eis elicere bona.
paras.en: [[1:22|In all these things|In omnibus his]], that is, his tribulations and adversities, [[1:22|Job sinned not by his lips|non peccavit Job labiis suis]], by speaking in a disordered, impatient or murmuring way: in which his perfection is plain, for, as James says, [[Jas 3:2|If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man|Si quis in verbo non offendit, hic perfectus est vir]]. [[1:22|nor spoke he any foolish thing against God|Neque stultum quid contra Deum locutus est]], that is, he uttered nothing contrary to true wisdom, which is the knowledge of divine things, as do some who are imperfect and given to passion, who, when they see or suffer something that seems to them very unreasonable and unjust, begin to doubt of God's providence and to pour out unseemly words. But blessed Job was not unaware that God is so good and wise that he would never let evils come about unless he knew how, willed, and was able to draw good out of them.

1.title: Elucidatio allegorica ejusdem capituli primi.
1.title_en: Allegorical explanation of the same first chapter

paras.t: Expositores, quos legi, parum aut nihil de mystica, id est allegorica et tropologica, expositione libri hujus scripserunt, forte quia B. Gregorius mysteria ejus diserte ac luculenter exposuit. Verum, quia Gregorius tractando diffusus atque prolixus est, nec omnibus est facultas ejus prælegantissima scripta ad manum habere, nec sic mysticum prosecutus est sensum, quin superbenignissimo ac supermunificentissimo Spiritu Sancto præstante, queant et alia dici ac aliqua addi, dicta quoque ab eo clarius exprimi; aliqua de spirituali ac mystico hujus voluminis intellectu, quantum paracletus Spiritus veritatis donaverit, scribere opto. Itaque a principio inchoandum videtur.
paras.en: The expositors whom I have read have written little or nothing on the mystical exposition of this book, that is, the allegorical and tropological [that is, the moral], perhaps because blessed Gregory expounded its mysteries clearly and brilliantly. But since Gregory is diffuse and lengthy in his treatment, and not everyone has the means of having his most elegant writings at hand, and since he has not so pursued the mystical sense that, by the gift of the most kind and most bountiful Holy Ghost, other things cannot be said and some things added, and what he said be expressed more clearly, I wish to write something on the spiritual and mystical understanding of this volume, so far as the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, shall grant. And so it seems we must begin from the beginning.

paras.t: Vir erat in terra Hus, nomine Job. Allegoria quid credendum sit, docet: tuncque potissime intellectus allegoricus est, dum quod litteraliter de antiquis dictum est patribus Christum præfigurantibus, de Christo exponitur. Porro, ut tactum est, Job verbis, tribulationibus, virtutibus, persona et nominis interpretatione Christum præfiguravit, sicut et Jeremias ac alii multi. Job quippe interpretatur dolens; Hus, sapientia.
paras.en: [[1:1|There was a man in the land of Hus, whose name was Job|Vir erat in terra Hus, nomine Job]]. Allegory teaches what is to be believed [an echo of the old verse on the senses of Scripture: the letter teaches what was done, allegory what to believe, the moral sense what to do, the anagogical where to tend]; and the understanding is most properly allegorical when what is said literally of the ancient fathers who prefigured Christ is expounded of Christ. Now, as was touched on, Job prefigured Christ by his words, his tribulations, his virtues, his person and the meaning of his name, as did Jeremias also and many others. For Job is interpreted sorrowing; Hus, wisdom.

paras.t: Itaque Vir, id est Christus, Deus et homo in una persona: qui ab instanti suæ incarnationis vir fuit, non corporis quantitate, sed virtutum perfectione, gratiarumque plenitudine; de quo per respectum ad ejus infantiam scriptum est in Jeremia, Novum creavit Dominus super terram, mulier circumdabit virum; de quo ut provectæ ætatis, in Actibus loquitur Petrus, Jesum Nazarenum, virum approbatum a Deo a signis et virtutibus et prodigiis, Deus suscitavit. Erat in terra Hus, id est Judæa, in qua sapientia, id est unius veri Dei cognitio cultusque, viguit, juxta quod scriptum est: Notus in Judæa Deus. Ibi enim Christus nasci et conversari ac mori elegit. Nomine Job: quod interpretatur dolens, id est Christus, cujus tota in hoc mundo vita doloribus plena fuit, quamvis anima ejus quoad suum supremum, in beatificæ fruitionis gaudio fuerit indesinenter ab incarnationis exordio. Hoc etenim non obstante, ab eodem exordio cœpit humano generi compati, de ejus peccatis tristari, corporis quoque pœnalitatibus aliquando affici; natus vero, cœpit mox multis modis affligi persecutioneque appeti, et tandem amarissimam passus est mortem. Propter quod Isaias de ipso conscribit: Vidimus eum despectum et novissimum virorum, virum dolorum et scientem infirmitatem. Qui ait in Psalmo: Super dolorem vulnerum meorum addiderunt. Itemque: Ego sum pauper et dolens. Denique anima Christi, quantum ad vires suas supremas, ad increatum objectum comparatas, et ipsæ vires sic comparatæ, fuerunt in perfecta felicitate et gaudio fruitionis beatæ, ut dictum est, incessanter ab incarnationis momento; sed anima ejus ut corporis forma, et vires ejus supremæ ad ipsam animam, cujus erant potentiæ, et ad creata objecta relatæ, fuerunt passibiles et in doloribus multis. De corporis autem et inferiorum virium animæ Christi passibilitate ac pœnis pro tempore ejus in hoc sæculo incolatus, minor est difficultas, nullumque dubium. Ex quibus patescit, quomodo Christus in vita præsenti mortali fuit simul viator et comprehensor.
paras.en: So: [[1:1|a man|Vir]], that is, Christ, God and man in one person, who from the instant of his incarnation was a man [Latin vir: a man in his full strength, not merely a human being], not in the size of his body, but in the perfection of his virtues and the fulness of his graces. Of him it is written in Jeremias, with regard to his infancy, [[Jer 31:22|the Lord hath created a new thing upon the earth: A WOMAN SHALL COMPASS A MAN|Novum creavit Dominus super terram, mulier circumdabit virum]]; of him as of mature age Peter speaks in the Acts: [[Acts 2:22|Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved of God among you by miracles and wonders and signs|Jesum Nazarenum, virum approbatum a Deo a signis et virtutibus et prodigiis]], [[Acts 2:24|God hath raised up|Deus suscitavit]]. He was [[1:1|in the land of Hus|in terra Hus]], that is, in Judea, in which wisdom, that is, the knowledge and worship of the one true God, flourished, according to what is written: [[Ps 75:2|In Judea God is known|Notus in Judæa Deus]]. For there Christ chose to be born, to live among men and to die. [[1:1|whose name was Job|Nomine Job]]: which is interpreted sorrowing, that is, Christ, whose whole life in this world was full of sorrows, though his soul, as to its highest part, was unceasingly in the joy of the beatific enjoyment [that is, the vision and possession of God that the blessed have] from the first moment of his incarnation. For notwithstanding this, from that same first moment he began to suffer with the human race, to be saddened over its sins, and at times also to be touched by bodily penalties [that is, the sufferings that are the penalty of sin]; and once born, he soon began to be afflicted in many ways and assailed with persecution, and at last he suffered a most bitter death. Therefore Isaias writes of him: [[Is 53:2|we have seen him|Vidimus eum]] [[Is 53:3|Despised, and the most abject of men, a man of sorrows, and acquainted with infirmity|despectum et novissimum virorum, virum dolorum et scientem infirmitatem]]. And he says in the Psalm: [[Ps 68:27|they have added to the grief of my wounds|Super dolorem vulnerum meorum addiderunt]]. And again: [[Ps 68:30|I am poor and sorrowful|Ego sum pauper et dolens]]. Further, the soul of Christ, as to its highest powers compared to their uncreated object, and those powers themselves so compared, were in perfect happiness and in the joy of blessed enjoyment, as was said, unceasingly from the moment of the incarnation; but his soul as the form of the body, and his highest powers as related to the soul itself, whose powers they were, and to created objects, were passible [that is, capable of suffering] and in many sorrows. And as to the passibility and the pains of Christ's body and of the lower powers of his soul during the time of his sojourn in this world, there is less difficulty, and no doubt at all. From this it is plain how Christ, in this present mortal life, was at once a wayfarer and a comprehensor [that is, both still on the way, as we are, and already in possession of the vision of God, as the blessed are].

paras.t: Hus insuper interpretatur consiliator. Job ergo in terra Hus fuit, id est, Christus in cordibus populi consilia recta sequentis quiescit, quemadmodum in Proverbiis Christus increata Dei Patris Sapientia, contestatur: Ego Sapientia habito in consilio, et eruditis intersum cogitationibus.
paras.en: Hus is interpreted, moreover, counsellor. So Job was in the land of Hus: that is, Christ rests in the hearts of a people that follows right counsels, as Christ, the uncreated Wisdom of God the Father, declares in the Proverbs: [[Prov 8:12|I, wisdom, dwell in counsel, and am present in learned thoughts|Ego Sapientia habito in consilio, et eruditis intersum cogitationibus]].

paras.t: Et erat vir ille, demonstrabilis, omni reverentia superdignissimus, simplex et rectus: quia secundum divinitatem, qua æqualis est Patri, est per essentiam supersimplicissima unitas, purusque actus et ipsa rectitudo seu æquitas, totius justitiæ ac virtutis regula et mensura. Porro secundum naturam assumptam fuit simplificatus in Deo, ita quod omnes suæ animæ affectiones erant impeccabiliter ordinatæ, reductæ, confirmatæ in eo. At vero (secundum Gregorium) per rectitudinem justitia, per simplicitatem mansuetudo accipitur. Nos autem plerumque quum rectitudinem justitiæ exsequimur, mansuetudinem relinquimus; quum mansuetudinem servare cupimus, a justitiæ rectitudine declinamus. Christus vero utrumque istorum in omnibus simul servavit ac optime temperavit.
paras.en: [[1:1|and that man|Et erat vir ille]] (the one to be pointed out [Denis takes ille, that, as pointing to him], worthy beyond all of every reverence) [[1:1|was simple and upright|simplex et rectus]]: because according to his Godhead, by which he is equal to the Father, he is by essence a unity more than supremely simple, pure act, and rectitude or equity itself, the rule and measure of all justice and virtue. And according to the nature he assumed, he was made simple in God, so that all the affections of his soul were ordered without possibility of sin, led back [to God] and confirmed in him. But (according to Gregory) by uprightness justice is meant, by simplicity gentleness. We, however, when we carry out the uprightness of justice, often abandon gentleness; when we wish to keep gentleness, we turn aside from the uprightness of justice. But Christ kept both of these together in all things, and tempered them perfectly.

paras.t: Ac timens Deum, filiali timore, ut homo, præsertim prout timor est donum, ejusque actus est Deum revereri; non autem timuit culpam incidere, sciens se confirmatum in bono. Timor autem, qui est donum, quoad actum qui est Deum revereri, manet in patria: unde de Christo prædictum est in Isaia, Replebit eum spiritus timoris Domini.
paras.en: [[1:1|and fearing God|Ac timens Deum]], with a filial fear, as man, and especially as fear is a gift [of the Holy Ghost], whose act is to revere God; but he did not fear to fall into sin, knowing himself confirmed in good. Now the fear that is a gift remains in the fatherland [that is, in heaven] as to the act which is to revere God[[Ps 18:10||]]: hence it was foretold of Christ in Isaias, [[Is 11:3|he shall be filled with the spirit of the fear of the Lord|Replebit eum spiritus timoris Domini]].

paras.t: Et recedens a malo culpæ, cui nunquam consensit, nec ipsum incurrit, ut Petrus princeps Apostolorum et Isaias flos Prophetarum testantur. Non autem recessit a malo pœnæ, id est malis pœnalibus: de quibus fatetur, Quia repleta est malis anima mea. Iste recessus Christi a malo culpæ fuit perversis Judæis occasio invidiæ contra eum, quemadmodum in libro Sapientiæ habetur: Dixerunt impii: Circumveniamus justum, quoniam contrarius est operibus nostris, et improperat nobis peccata legis; promittit se scientiam Dei habere, et filium Dei se nominat. Tanquam nugaces æstimati sumus ab eo, et abstinet se a viis nostris tanquam ab immunditiis, et gloriatur se Deum patrem habere.
paras.en: [[1:1|and avoiding evil|Et recedens a malo]], the evil of sin, to which he never consented, nor did he incur it, as Peter, the prince of the Apostles[[1 Pet 2:22||]][[Acts 3:14||]], and Isaias, the flower of the Prophets[[Is 53:9||]], testify [the margin's reference to the Acts is partly illegible; Acts 3:14 is the likeliest]. But he did not withdraw from the evil of punishment, that is, from penal evils: of which he confesses, [[Ps 87:4|For my soul is filled with evils|Quia repleta est malis anima mea]]. This withdrawal of Christ from the evil of sin was to the perverse Jews an occasion of envy against him, as we find in the book of Wisdom: The wicked said[[Wis 2:1||]]: [[Wis 2:12|Let us, therefore, lie in wait for the just|Circumveniamus justum]], [[Wis 2:12|because|quoniam]] [[Wis 2:12|he is contrary to our doings, and upbraideth us with transgressions of the law|contrarius est operibus nostris, et improperat nobis peccata legis]]; [[Wis 2:13|He boasteth that he hath the knowledge of God, and calleth himself the son of God|promittit se scientiam Dei habere, et filium Dei se nominat]]. [[Wis 2:16|We are esteemed by him as triflers, and he abstaineth from our ways as from filthiness|Tanquam nugaces æstimati sumus ab eo, et abstinet se a viis nostris tanquam ab immunditiis]], [[Wis 2:16|and glorieth that he hath God for his father|et gloriatur se Deum patrem habere]].

paras.t: Natique sunt ei, spirituali generatione per fidelium multiplicationem in susceptione Baptismatis seu infusione superni charismatis, septem filii, id est universitas Christianorum. Septenario enim perfectio universitasque signantur: sic namque in Apocalypsi per septem spiritus, et in Tobia per septem coram Deo adstantes, universitas angelorum exprimitur. Et tres filiæ: per quas specialiter designantur congregationes religiosæ, Deo in fide superbeatissimæ Trinitatis devotissime servientes. Vel, septem filii sunt catalogus Apostolorum virtutibus perfectorum; tres filiæ, inferiorum status fidelium, ut pastorum, et continentium, ac conjugatorum. De hac Christi generatione in Isaia scriptum est: Si posuerit animam suam pro peccato, videbit semen longævum. Et ipsemet Christus: Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua et Spiritu Sancto, non potest introire in regnum Dei.
paras.en: [[1:2|And there were born to him|Natique sunt ei]], by a spiritual generation, through the multiplying of the faithful in the receiving of Baptism or the infusion of heavenly grace, [[1:2|seven sons|septem filii]], that is, the whole body of Christians. For by the number seven perfection and universality are signified: so in the Apocalypse by the seven spirits[[Apoc 1:4||]], and in Tobias by the seven who stand before God[[Tob 12:15||]], the whole body of the angels is expressed. [[1:2|and three daughters|Et tres filiæ]]: by whom are signified in particular the religious congregations, which serve God most devoutly in the faith of the most supremely blessed Trinity. Or the seven sons are the roll of the Apostles, perfect in virtues; the three daughters, the lower states of the faithful, as of pastors, of the continent and of the married. Of this generation of Christ it is written in Isaias: [[Is 53:10|if he shall lay down his life for sin, he shall see a longlived seed|Si posuerit animam suam pro peccato, videbit semen longævum]]. And Christ himself: [[John 3:5|unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Ghost, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God|Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua et Spiritu Sancto, non potest introire in regnum Dei]].

paras.t: Et fuit possessio ejus septem millia ovium. Quamvis omnia sint Christi secundum suam divinitatem jure creationis, omnia quoque ejus humanitati subjecta sint potissime ob hypostaticam ejus cum Verbo unionem, quidam tamen homines specialiter Christi esse dicuntur per prædestinationem et gratiam. De quibus fatetur: Omne quod dat mihi Pater, ad me veniet. Apostolus quoque ad Ephesios: Deus elegit nos in Christo ante mundi constitutionem. Et iterum: Prædestinavit nos in adoptionem filiorum per Jesum Christum secundum propositum voluntatis suæ. Hi autem secundum diversas suas proprietates atque virtutes, diversis animalium nominibus designantur, etiam interdum ad litteram, ut in Isaia, quo habetur: Habitabit lupus cum agno, et pardus cum hœdo accubabit; vitulus, ovis et leo simul morabuntur.
