Christ too, when his passion was at hand, says: There cometh to me [[John 14:30|the prince of this world|princeps mundi]], [[John 14:30|and in me he hath not any thing|et in me non habet quidquam]]. And again he says to the Jews: [[John 8:44|You are of your father the devil|Vos ex patre diabolo estis]]: [[John 8:44|and the desires of your father you will do|et desideria patris vestri vultis perficere]], by killing me. And again, having described the threefold temptation of Christ, begun in the desert, Luke added: [[Luke 4:13|And all the temptation being ended, the devil departed from him for a time|Consummata omni tentatione, diabolus recessit ab eo usque ad tempus]]: by which he hints that the devil afterwards returned, not, to be sure, without God’s leave and permission. From all this it is in great part plain how the present chapter applies to Christ. Some of the harder points, however, must be touched upon.

paras.t: Ait itaque Deus ad Satan: Commovisti me adversus eum. Secundum Gregorium, per hoc Satan commovit Patrem adversus Christum, quod Satan in paradiso induxit primum hominem ad peccatum, pro cujus expiatione Deus Pater Christum Filium suum tentari atque occidi permisit. Verumtamen sicut præcedenti capitulo istud expositum est de Job, ita de Christo potest exponi, ut Pater loquens more humano dicat se a Satan commotum ad affligendum Christum, in quantum hoc ex rationabili causa permisit ad expetitionem Satan; et quod ait, Adversus eum, non denotat discordiam aliquam inter Patrem et Filium, sicut nec inter Deum et Job, sed quod permissio ista fuit afflictiva ipsius Christi, in quantum per eam diabolus incitavit Judæos ad Christi persecutionem. Ut affligerem, id est, a Judæis membris atque satellitibus tuis, o Satan, affligi permitterem, eum frustra, id est sine ipsius culpa, quia peccatum non fecit; vel, frustra, quoad tuam intentionem, quia persequendo in eo nil profecisti, sed potius defecisti, sicut expositum est plenius præcedenti articulo. Ad istud allegat Gregorius, quod in libro Sapientiæ dicitur Deo: Quum sis justus, juste omnia disponis; eum quoque qui non debet puniri, condemnas. Christus enim puniri pro se ipso non debuit. Pater ergo quum sit justus, omnia juste disponit: quia per hoc cuncta justificat, quod eum qui sine peccato est, pro peccatoribus morti tradidit.
paras.en: God then says to Satan: [[2:3|thou hast moved me against him|Commovisti me adversus eum]]. According to Gregory, Satan moved the Father against Christ in this, that in paradise Satan led the first man into sin, for the expiation of which God the Father allowed Christ his Son to be tempted and slain. But just as this was explained of Job in the preceding chapter [that is, in the literal exposition of this chapter, in the preceding article], so it can be explained of Christ: the Father, speaking in human fashion, says that he was moved by Satan to afflict Christ, inasmuch as for a reasonable cause he allowed this at Satan’s request; and when he says, [[2:3|against him|Adversus eum]], this does not denote any discord between the Father and the Son, as neither between God and Job, but that this permission brought affliction on Christ himself, inasmuch as through it the devil stirred up the Jews to persecute Christ. [[2:3|that I should afflict him|Ut affligerem]], that is, that I should allow him to be afflicted by the Jews, thy members and henchmen, O Satan; [[2:3|without cause|eum frustra]], that is, without any fault of his own, since he is one [[1 Pet 2:22|Who did no sin|peccatum non fecit]]; or, in vain [frustra means both “without cause” and “in vain”], as regards thy intention, for by persecuting him thou didst gain nothing in him, but rather didst fail, as was explained more fully in the preceding article. To this Gregory applies what is said to God in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 12:15|For so much then, as thou art just, thou orderest all things justly|Quum sis justus, juste omnia disponis]]; and him also who ought not to be punished thou condemnest [so Gregory reads; the Vulgate and the Douay-Rheims say the opposite, that God thinks it foreign to his power to condemn him who ought not to be punished]. For Christ ought not to have been punished for himself. The Father therefore, since he is just, orders all things justly: for he justifies all things by this, that he delivered up to death for sinners him who is without sin.

paras.t: Respondit Satan: Pellem pro pelle, etc. His verbis, juxta interpretationem præhabitam, Satan vult dicere, quod licet Christus de aliorum dejectione atque periculo per impatientiam victus non sit, vinceretur tamen per eam, si in proprio corpore usque ad ossa percuteretur, æstimans quod purus fuisset homo et Propheta dumtaxat, non etiam Dominus Prophetarum omniumque Salvator. Alioqui mitte manum tuam, et tange os ejus et carnem, id est, flagellari eum permitte usque ad interiora. Hæc Satan quum per se fieri petiit, desiderans dixit; per membra sua hæc, id est, per Judæos incredulos, verbis ac desideriis intulit: sicque permissionem persequendi Christum usque ad crucis patibulum postulavit.
paras.en: [[2:4|And Satan answered|Respondit Satan]]: [[2:4|Skin for skin|Pellem pro pelle]], etc. By these words, according to the interpretation given before, Satan means that although Christ had not been overcome by impatience over the overthrow and peril of others, he would yet be overcome by it if he were struck in his own body even to the bones; for he thought that he was a mere man and only a Prophet, not also the Lord of all the Prophets and the Saviour of all. [[2:5|But put forth thy hand, and touch his bone and his flesh|Alioqui mitte manum tuam, et tange os ejus et carnem]], that is, allow him to be scourged even to the inward parts. When Satan asked for these things to be done through himself, he spoke them out of desire; through his members, that is, through the unbelieving Jews, he brought them about in words and desires: and so he asked leave to persecute Christ even to the gibbet of the cross.

paras.t: Dicit ergo Dominus ad Satan: Ecce in manu tua est, id est, permitto ut tua suggestione per tua membra eum affligas, flagelles, occidas. Proprio enim Filio suo non pepercit Deus, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit illum, ut dicit Apostolus. Ideo in Isaia ait: Propter scelus populi mei percussi eum. Verumtamen animam illius serva, id est, animæ ejus nequaquam nocebis, nec per passionis acerbitatem rationis in ea judicium obrues: juxta illud in Psalmo, Nihil proficiet inimicus in eo, et filius iniquitatis non apponet nocere ei. Unde quod ait, Animam illius serva, intelligendum est potius prænuntiative quam prohibitive: quia etsi Pater tunc non prohibuisset, non tamen Satan Christi animam ad culpam unquam inducere valuisset.
paras.en: [[2:6|And the Lord said to Satan|Dicit ergo Dominus ad Satan]]: [[2:6|Behold, he is in thy hand|Ecce in manu tua est]], that is, I allow thee, at thy prompting and through thy members, to afflict him, to scourge him, to slay him. For God [[Rom 8:32|spared not even his own Son|Proprio enim Filio suo non pepercit Deus]], [[Rom 8:32|but delivered him up for us all|sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit illum]], as the Apostle says. Therefore he says in Isaias: [[Is 53:8|for the wickedness of my people have I struck him|Propter scelus populi mei percussi eum]]. [[2:6|but yet save his life|Verumtamen animam illius serva]] [anima, “life”, is also “soul”, and Denis takes it so], that is, thou shalt in no way harm his soul, nor by the bitterness of the passion overwhelm the judgment of reason in it: according to that in the Psalm, [[Ps 88:23|The enemy shall have no advantage over him: nor the son of iniquity have power to hurt him|Nihil proficiet inimicus in eo, et filius iniquitatis non apponet nocere ei]]. Hence when he says, [[2:6|save his life|Animam illius serva]], it is to be understood as a foretelling rather than a forbidding: for even if the Father had not then forbidden it, Satan would never have been able to lead Christ’s soul into sin.

paras.t: Egressus igitur Satan a facie Domini, percussit Job ulcere pessimo, id est, Christum gravissime vulnerari ac percuti procuravit in die Parasceves per totum corpus ipsius sanctissimum, ita ut dicat percussus: O vos omnes qui transitis per viam, attendite, et videte si est dolor similis sicut dolor meus. Dixerunt enim iniqui: Morte turpissima condemnemus eum. Qui testa saniem radebat; quoniam tempore passionis sæpe proprio digito igne passionis instar testæ intus siccato atque durato, sputa et sanguinem defluentem ex oculis suis detersit. Porro, secundum Gregorium, testa saniem radebat, id est, peccatum generis humani carne sua delevit: quæ caro in passione velut testa induruit. Sedens in sterquilinio, id est in loco Calvariæ sordido, antequam cruci affigeretur.
paras.en: [[2:7|So Satan went forth from the presence of the Lord|Egressus igitur Satan a facie Domini]], [[2:7|and struck Job with a very grievous ulcer|percussit Job ulcere pessimo]], that is, he brought it about that Christ was most grievously wounded and struck, on the day of the Parasceve [the day of preparation, Good Friday], over the whole of his most holy body[[John 19:1||]], so that, stricken, he says: [[Lam 1:12|O all ye that pass by the way, attend, and see if there be any sorrow like to my sorrow|O vos omnes qui transitis per viam, attendite, et videte si est dolor similis sicut dolor meus]]. For the wicked said: [[Wis 2:20|Let us condemn him to a most shameful death|Morte turpissima condemnemus eum]]. [[2:8|And he took a potsherd and scraped the corrupt matter|Qui testa saniem radebat]]: because in the time of the passion, with his own finger, dried and hardened within like a potsherd by the fire of the passion, he often wiped away the spittle and the blood that flowed down from his eyes. Further, according to Gregory, [[2:8|he took a potsherd and scraped the corrupt matter|testa saniem radebat]], that is, he blotted out the sin of the human race with his flesh, which flesh in the passion hardened like a potsherd[[Ps 21:16||]]. [[2:8|sitting on a dunghill|Sedens in sterquilinio]], that is, in the filthy place of Calvary, before he was fastened to the cross.

paras.t: Dixit autem illi uxor sua, id est Synagoga, aliquando Dei sponsa, sed tunc facta adultera, diabolo consentiens et commixta: Adhuc permanes in simplicitate, id est stoliditate tua? prout simplicitas perspicacitati intellectus opponitur. Putabat equidem perfida Synagoga, quod Jesus ex insipientia fateretur se Christum Deique Filium. Benedic Deo, negando te Filium ejus. Quasi dicat: Injuriam Deo fecisti, te ejus Filium perhibendo; nunc ergo da gloriam ei, et abnega quod dixisti. Et morere, ne alios deinceps decipias, id est, penitus pereas. Qui ait ad illam: Quasi una de stultis mulieribus locuta es. Sic Christus increpavit Synagogam, dicendo: Si dixero quia non novi Deum, ero vobis similis, mendax. Et item quum caperetur: Tanquam ad latronem existis cum gladiis et fustibus comprehendere me; quotidie apud vos eram in templo docens, et non me tenuistis. Sed hæc est hora vestra et potestas tenebrarum. Si bona suscepimus de manu Domini, mala quare non sustineamus? Hoc Christus loquitur ex parte naturæ assumptæ, quam Deus omni creaturæ præfecit, quemadmodum in Joanne scriptum est: Sciens Jesus quia omnia dedit ei Pater in manus. Et alibi: Omnia mihi tradita sunt a Patre meo. Vult itaque dicere: Quum Pater mihi omnia subjecerit, meamque humanitatem Verbo æterno unierit, cur pro hominibus mori non debeam, pro quorum salute recuperanda Pater tot bona mihi secundum assumptam humanitatem donavit? Non ergo propter pœnarum acerbitatem a bona simplicitate mea recedere debeo, ut Christum Deique Filium esse me negem, o insipiens Synagoga.
paras.en: [[2:9|And his wife said to him|Dixit autem illi uxor sua]], that is, the Synagogue, once the bride of God, but then become an adulteress, consenting to the devil and joined with him: [[2:9|Dost thou still continue in thy simplicity|Adhuc permanes in simplicitate]], that is, thy stolidity? taking simplicity as it is opposed to keenness of understanding. For the faithless Synagogue thought that Jesus, out of folly, professed himself to be the Christ and the Son of God. [[2:9|bless God|Benedic Deo]], by denying that thou art his Son. As if to say: Thou hast done God a wrong by calling thyself his Son; now therefore give glory to him, and deny what thou hast said. [[2:9|and die|Et morere]], lest thou deceive others hereafter, that is, perish utterly. [[2:10|And he said to her: Thou hast spoken like one of the foolish women|Qui ait ad illam: Quasi una de stultis mulieribus locuta es]]. So Christ rebuked the Synagogue, saying: [[John 8:55|And if I shall say that I know him not, I shall be like to you, a liar|Si dixero quia non novi Deum, ero vobis similis, mendax]]. And again, when he was being taken: [[Matt 26:55|You are come out, as it were to a robber, with swords and clubs to apprehend me|Tanquam ad latronem existis cum gladiis et fustibus comprehendere me]]; [[Matt 26:55|I sat daily with you, teaching in the temple: and you laid not hands on me|quotidie apud vos eram in templo docens, et non me tenuistis]]. [[Luke 22:53|but this is your hour and the power of darkness|Sed hæc est hora vestra et potestas tenebrarum]]. [[2:10|If we have received good things at the hand of God, why should we not receive evil?|Si bona suscepimus de manu Domini, mala quare non sustineamus?]] Christ says this on the part of the nature he assumed, which God set over every creature, as it is written in John: [[John 13:3|Knowing that the Father had given him all things into his hands|Sciens Jesus quia omnia dedit ei Pater in manus]]. And elsewhere: [[Matt 11:27|All things are delivered to me by my Father|Omnia mihi tradita sunt a Patre meo]]. He means, then: Since the Father has subjected all things to me, and has united my humanity to the eternal Word, why should I not die for men, for the recovery of whose salvation the Father has given me so many good things according to the humanity I assumed? I must not therefore, because of the bitterness of the pains, depart from my good simplicity so as to deny that I am the Christ and the Son of God, O foolish Synagogue.

paras.t: Igitur audientes tres amici Job omne malum quod accidisset ei. Quidam per istos Job sancti amicos intelligendos putant hæreticos: quod licet in sequentibus stet, tamen hoc loco non multum apparet, præsertim quum hæretici non sint Christi amici, nec ei vere condoleant, neque se passioni ipsius vere conforment. Aptius itaque reor, per istos amicos hoc loco, in quo bona egisse scribuntur, intelligi Christianos, qui ex evangelica historia seu prædicatione Ecclesiæ audientes universa quæ pro ipsis Christus pertulerit, pariter statuunt et condicunt, ut ad loca sacra ubi dominicæ passionis commemoratio agitur, veniant, et Christi passionem, quasi præsentialiter fiat, oculis suæ mentis proponant; consolenturque Christum, confitendo ejus innocentiam et suas malitias, quod item non pro suis, sed pro eorum ista patiatur peccatis; eique gratias agant, et compassionem exhibeant cordialem. A longe quoque videntes imaginem ejus in cruce erectam, quasi ipsum in cruce videant elevatum, vestimenta sua mox scindant, id est, pristina opera vitiosa, quibus se impie operuerunt, prorsus abjiciant, pœnitendoque destruant, et præ compassione exclament ac plorent. Sed et super capita sua pulverem spargant, id est, cogitationes, affectiones, et actus humilitatis ac pœnitentiæ cruciformisque conversationis, suis superjaciant cordibus. Insuper sedeant secum, de se ipsis humilia sentiendo, a mundi inquietudinibus recedendo, meditationibus insistendo, septem diebus et septem noctibus, id est per omne tempus vitæ suæ in sæculo isto, omni videlicet die et nocte et congruentibus horis: septenario nempe universitas designatur. Nemo quoque loquitur ei verbum de non patiendo seu passione et morte vitanda, ne audiat quod Christus Petro passionis vitationem persuadenti locutus est: Vade retro me, Satana: non sapis quæ Dei sunt, sed quæ hominum.
paras.en: [[2:11|Now when Job's three friends heard all the evil that had befallen him|Igitur audientes tres amici Job omne malum quod accidisset ei]]. Some think that by these friends of holy Job heretics are to be understood: and though this may hold in what follows, at this place it is not very apparent, especially since heretics are not Christ’s friends, and do not truly grieve with him, nor truly conform themselves to his passion. I think it more fitting, then, that by these friends, at this place, where they are written to have done good things, Christians are understood: who, hearing from the gospel history or the preaching of the Church all that Christ endured for them, together resolve and agree to come to the holy places where the commemoration of the Lord’s passion is kept, and to set Christ’s passion before the eyes of their mind as though it were happening before them; and to comfort Christ, by confessing his innocence and their own wickedness, and that he suffers these things not for his own sins but for theirs; and to give him thanks, and show him heartfelt compassion. Seeing also [[2:12|afar off|A longe]] his image set up on the cross, as if they saw him lifted up on the cross, let them at once rend their garments, that is, cast off utterly, and destroy by doing penance, the vicious works of the past with which they wickedly clothed themselves; and out of compassion let them cry out and weep. And let them also sprinkle dust upon their heads, that is, cast upon their hearts thoughts, affections and acts of humility and of penance and of a life shaped by the cross. Moreover let them sit with him, thinking humbly of themselves, withdrawing from the disquiet of the world, applying themselves to meditation, [[2:13|seven day and seven nights|septem diebus et septem noctibus]], that is, through all the time of their life in this world, namely every day and night and at the fitting hours: for by the number seven the whole is signified. And [[2:13|no man spoke to him a word|Nemo quoque loquitur ei verbum]] about not suffering, or about avoiding the passion and death, lest he hear what Christ said to Peter when he urged him to avoid the passion: [[Mark 8:33|Go behind me, Satan|Vade retro me, Satana]], [[Mark 8:33|thou savourest not the things that are of God but that are of men|non sapis quæ Dei sunt, sed quæ hominum]][[Matt 16:23||]].

paras.t: Præterea quæ de tropologico hujus capituli intellectu dici possent, videntur mihi ex dictis patere; congruitque brevitati studere. Cuilibet equidem justo quem Deus aliquando permisit tentari, nec desiit suffragari, sed vincere fecit, possunt prædicta secundum sensum de Job positum applicari. Videns etenim Satan aliquem divitiarum suarum ac omnium ad se pertinentium ablationem forti patientia ferre, atque in Dei reverentia permanere, petit a Domino ut permittat talem in propria persona infirmitatibus ac doloribus intime affici, præsumens quod talia sine impatientia et murmuratione non patietur; conceditque Dominus sic fieri. Porro vir justus et timoratus sciens Deum dixisse, Ego quos amo, arguo et castigo, et quod multa graviora pati meruerit uno peccato mortali, quam sint cuncta mundi hujus supplicia, patientiam grata mente conservat, manumque juvat exedentis, et pro viribus actibus pœnitentiæ se exercet, simul et illud Apostoli pensans: Quia si compatimur, et conregnabimus, et quod non sunt condignæ passiones hujus temporis ad futuram gloriam patientibus dandam. Itaque testa saniem radit, id est, pœnitentiali rigore ac justa districtione vitiorum suorum putredinem delet; sedens in sterquilinio, id est, in propriæ vilitatis vel immundæ vitæ prioris carnalis profunda consideratione quiescens, non in alto elationis ac vanitatis se ponens, sed cogitans, Quid superbit terra et cinis? Cur contra Deum insanit peccator? Cur vermis tam fragilis sibi quidquam nisi defectuositatem omnem adscribit?
paras.en: As for what could be said of the tropological sense of this chapter, it seems to me to be plain from what has been said; and it is fitting to aim at brevity. For what has been said according to the sense given of Job can be applied to any just man whom God has at some time allowed to be tempted, and has not ceased to help, but has made to overcome. For when Satan sees someone bearing with strong patience the loss of his riches and of all that belongs to him, and remaining in the reverence of God, he asks the Lord to allow such a man to be afflicted inwardly in his own person with sicknesses and pains, presuming that he will not suffer such things without impatience and murmuring; and the Lord grants that it be so. But the just and God-fearing man, knowing that God has said, [[Apoc 3:19|Such as I love, I rebuke and chastise|Ego quos amo, arguo et castigo]], and that by a single mortal sin he has deserved to suffer things far heavier than all the punishments of this world, keeps his patience with a grateful mind, and helps the hand of him that wears him down [exedentis; perhaps a misprint or misreading for cædentis, “of him that strikes”], and exercises himself as far as he can in acts of penance, weighing at the same time that saying of the Apostle: [[2 Tim 2:12|If we suffer, we shall also reign with him|si compatimur, et conregnabimus]][[Rom 8:17||]] [Denis’s words join Rom 8:17, “if we suffer with him”, to 2 Tim 2:12, “we shall also reign with him”], and that [[Rom 8:18|the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come|non sunt condignæ passiones hujus temporis ad futuram gloriam]] that is to be given to those who suffer. And so he [[2:8|took a potsherd and scraped the corrupt matter|testa saniem radit]], that is, by penitential rigour and just severity he blots out the rottenness of his vices; [[2:8|sitting on a dunghill|sedens in sterquilinio]], that is, resting in deep consideration of his own vileness, or of the uncleanness of his former carnal life, not setting himself on the height of pride and vanity, but thinking: [[Ecclus 10:9|Why is earth, and ashes proud?|Quid superbit terra et cinis?]] Why does the sinner rage against God? Why does so frail a worm ascribe anything to himself but every kind of defect?

paras.t: Cui frequenter loquitur uxor sua, id est carnalis cognatio, aut sæcularis prudentia, seu passio appetitivæ potentiæ sensitivæ: Adhuc permanes in simplicitate tua? Carnales namque et sæculares passionalesque animi motus, non intelligentes quæ Dei sunt, dum justo ac pœnitenti vident aut sentiunt adversa contingere, putant supervacuum esse virtutibus insudare, et concupiscentiis eligunt consentire, vanitatibusque vacare. Hanc sensualitatem carnalemque sensum et falsam prudentiam ratio increpet atque erudiat, dicens: Quasi una de stultis mulieribus locuta es. Stulti quippe non nisi præsentia ac apparentia solent attendere; sapientium vero est, oculos cordis ad futura dirigere, ad interiora convertere, æternis infigere. Si bona suscepimus de manu, id est liberalitate omnipotentis, Domini, mala quare non sustineamus?
paras.en: To him his wife often speaks, that is, his carnal kindred, or worldly prudence, or the passion of the sensitive appetitive power: [[2:9|Dost thou still continue in thy simplicity?|Adhuc permanes in simplicitate tua?]] For the carnal and worldly and passionate movements of the soul, not understanding the things that are of God, when they see or feel adversity befall the just and penitent man, think it useless to toil at the virtues, and choose to consent to concupiscence and to give themselves to vanities. Let reason rebuke and instruct this sensuality and carnal sense and false prudence, saying: [[2:10|Thou hast spoken like one of the foolish women|Quasi una de stultis mulieribus locuta es]]. For fools are wont to attend only to things present and apparent; but it is for the wise to direct the eyes of the heart to things to come, to turn them to things within, to fix them on things eternal. [[2:10|If we have received good things at the hand|Si bona suscepimus de manu]], that is, from the liberality, of the almighty Lord, [[2:10|why should we not receive evil?|mala quare non sustineamus?]]

paras.t: Postremo, tres amici istius afflicti, qui audientes quæ passus sit, condicunt sibi ut pariter venientes consolentur et visitent eum, intelligi possunt triplex hominum status, vel triplex sapientia, utpote intellectus seu actualis intellectio legis tripartitæ, videlicet legis naturalis et scriptæ ac evangelicæ: quarum quælibet proponit remedia adversitatum consolativa, potissime intellectus evangelicæ legis, in qua quisque tanto prædicatur beatior, quanto propter Deum patienter afflictior. Isti amici exclamant, plorant, vestesque scindunt, et pulverem capiti superponunt, quoniam vires animæ sic agere faciunt juxta sensus prætactos. Postremo, isti amici intelligi queunt intellectus, affectus, memoria. Intellectus consolatur per sapientiam, futurique præmii considerationem, et intuendo quantus in æquanimi adversitatum tolerantia consistat profectus. Affectus seu ipse intellectivus appetitus, qui voluntas vocatur, consolatur per caritatem, jubens omnia patientissime ferri ex puro Dei amore, quoniam ei sic placet, et quoniam sæpe offendimus eum, atque ut Christo aliqualiter conformemur, in gratia quoque nunc et tandem in gloria concrescamus. Memoria seu vigor memorativus consolatur, ad mentem reducens quanta passus sit Christus, et omnes electi, qui frequenter quo suo Creatori cariores fuerunt, eo duriora perpessi sunt. Isti sunt interiores nostri amici, in quos dolor animæ nostræ redundat, residentque constanter cum ea, vestes suas scindentes, id est actiones sibi ante delectabiles penitus abhorrentes ac abjectantes: sed et pulverem sibi protinus superponunt, quia recordationibus, cogitatibus, affectibusque ad humilia et abjecta spectantibus simul intendunt; qui consolationem quoque interdum ad tempus suspendunt, horam congruam præstolantes, quousque consolationis mens fiat capacior.
paras.en: Lastly, the three friends of this afflicted man, who, hearing what he has suffered, agree among themselves to come together to comfort and visit him, can be understood as the threefold state of men, or a threefold wisdom: namely the understanding, or actual grasp, of the threefold law, that is, the natural law, the written law and the law of the Gospel; each of which sets forth remedies to console in adversity, but above all the understanding of the law of the Gospel, in which each man is proclaimed the more blessed the more patiently he is afflicted for God’s sake. These friends cry out, weep, rend their garments and put dust upon their heads, since they make the powers of the soul act so, in the senses touched on above. Or, lastly, these friends can be understood as the understanding, the affection and the memory. The understanding consoles through wisdom and the consideration of the reward to come, and by seeing how great a progress lies in bearing adversity with an even mind. The affection, or the intellective appetite itself, which is called the will, consoles through charity, bidding us bear all things most patiently out of the pure love of God: since so it pleases him, and since we have often offended him, and so that we may in some measure be conformed to Christ, and may grow in grace now and at length in glory. The memory, or the power of remembering, consoles by bringing back to mind how much Christ suffered, and all the elect, who often suffered the harder things the dearer they were to their Creator. These are our inward friends, into whom the grief of our soul overflows; and they sit constantly with it, rending their garments, that is, utterly abhorring and casting off the actions that before were pleasant to them; and they also at once put dust upon themselves, for together they attend to remembrances, thoughts and affections that look to lowly and abject things; and at times they also put off consolation for a while, awaiting the fitting hour, until the mind become more capable of consolation.

paras.t: Hæc de mysticis intellectibus tetigisse potius quam determinasse sufficiat. Gregorius autem mysteria spiritualis intelligentiæ prosequitur copiose, alios ponens sensus quam istos quos tetigi.
paras.en: Let it suffice to have touched on these things concerning the mystical senses, rather than to have settled them. Gregory, however, follows out the mysteries of the spiritual understanding at length, setting down other senses than those I have touched on.

3.title: Expositio capituli tertii: Post hæc aperuit Job os suum, et maledixit diei suo.
3.title_en: Exposition of the third chapter: After this Job opened his mouth, and cursed his day

paras.t: Elucidandum modo capitulum, difficultatibus plenum est. Circa cujus expositionem doctores sancti et magni atque catholici satis diversimode scripsisse atque sensisse monstrantur: quorum in primis positiones compendiosius quo potero, referre intendo. Beatus ergo Gregorius, qui librum istum asserit ante se indiscussum fuisse, eumque præclare exponit litteraliter, quantum fieri posse existimat, allegorice quoque et tropologice, protestatur multa in libro hoc contineri, præsertim in isto capitulo, quæ ad litteram exponi nequeunt. Porro S. Thomas et quidam eum sequentes, exponi posse hæc dicunt ad litteram, litteraliterque exponunt. Alberti autem Magni expositio videtur hinc inde obscura, sicut patebit. Videtur demum sentire litteraliter posse ista exponi, quamvis expositionem hujusmodi non admodum lucide prosequatur.
paras.en: The chapter now to be explained is full of difficulties. On its exposition the holy, great and Catholic doctors are found to have written and thought in rather different ways; and first of all I intend to relate their positions as briefly as I can. Blessed Gregory, then, who asserts that this book had not been discussed before him, and who expounds it excellently according to the letter, as far as he thinks this can be done, and also allegorically and tropologically [that is, in the moral sense], declares that many things are contained in this book, especially in this chapter, which cannot be expounded according to the letter. St Thomas, however, and some who follow him, say that these things can be expounded according to the letter, and expound them literally. The exposition of Albert the Great seems obscure here and there, as will appear. In the end he seems to hold that these things can be expounded literally, although he does not carry out an exposition of this kind very clearly.

paras.t: Primo igitur ponenda sunt motiva Gregorii, ejusque interpretatio inducenda. Itaque ait in prologo primi voluminis super Job: Aliquando, ne intelligi juxta litteram debeant, ipsa se litteræ verba impugnant. Ait namque, Pereat dies in qua natus sum, etc., qui dies jam evolutus, stare non poterat: quomodo ergo hunc perire et involvi caligine optat? In exordio autem quarti libri Moralium, ubi verba hæc exponere incepit, ait: Ecce quod beatus Job diei suo maledixisse describitur. Si superficie tenus attenditur, quid his verbis reprehensibilius invenitur? Hinc refert, quod istud nullo modo de die sensibili dicitur, quia et multa secundum litteram impossibilia subsequuntur, ut quod ait, Dies illa vertatur in tenebras, et involvatur amaritudine. Sit nox illa solitaria. Exspectet lucem, etc. Multa quoque secundum Gregorium, impossibilitatem litteraliter continent et irrationabiliter sonant, imo videntur verba hominis non solum impatientis, sed insuper desperantis, sicut quum ait: Quare non in vulva mortuus sum? etc. Hinc infert Gregorius: Quia igitur verba hæc in superficie a ratione discordant, ipsa jam littera indicat, quod in eis sanctus vir juxta litteram nihil dicat. Ponenda ergo nunc est expositio S. Gregorii.
paras.en: First, then, Gregory's reasons must be set out, and his interpretation brought in. He says, in the prologue of the first volume on Job: Sometimes the very words of the letter contradict themselves, so that they may not be understood according to the letter. For he says, [[3:3|Let the day perish wherein I was born|Pereat dies in qua natus sum]], etc.; and that day, having already rolled by, could not stand still: how then does he wish it to perish and to be wrapped in mist? And at the beginning of the fourth book of the Morals, where he begins to expound these words, he says: Behold, blessed Job is described as having cursed his day. If this is taken at the surface, what is found more blameworthy than these words? Hence he relates that this is in no way said of the day perceived by the senses, since many things impossible according to the letter follow, as when he says, [[3:4|Let that day be turned into darkness|Dies illa vertatur in tenebras]], [[3:5|and let it be wrapped up in bitterness|et involvatur amaritudine]]. [[3:7|Let that night be solitary|Sit nox illa solitaria]]. [[3:9|let it expect light|Exspectet lucem]], etc. Many things too, according to Gregory, contain an impossibility in the literal sense and sound unreasonable; nay, they seem the words of a man not only impatient but even despairing, as when he says: [[3:11|Why did I not die in the womb?|Quare non in vulva mortuus sum?]] etc. Hence Gregory infers: Since therefore these words on the surface are at odds with reason, the letter itself already shows that in them the holy man says nothing according to the letter. Now, then, the exposition of St Gregory must be set out.

paras.t: Post hæc aperuit Job os suum, et maledixit diei suo, et dixit: Pereat dies in qua natus sum, et nox in qua dictum est, Conceptus est homo. Solerter intuendum est quod dicitur, Post hæc, ut virtus rei quæ agitur, veraciter ex tempore sentiatur. Prius namque rerum ablatio, filiorum exstinctio, corporis læsio, persuasio conjugis, amicorum adventus, et quid egerunt, atque quod ibidem septem diebus sederunt, describitur; deinde subjungitur, Post hæc aperuit Job os suum, etc., ut ipso narrationis ordine perpendatur, quod maledictum nequaquam per impatientiam protulit. Si enim ira motus malediceret, auditis et illatis prædictis incommodis maledixisset; in quibus tamen gratias egit, conjugem increpavit, atque ad patientiam erudivit. Mente ergo quieta hæc dixit, qui tot Dei laudes etiam percussus pronuntiavit. Sciendum vero, quod secundum Scripturam maledictio duobus fit modis, scilicet bene, quando profertur zelo seu judicio justitiæ; et male, quando profertur livore vindictæ. Primo modo Dominus ait in Genesi: Maledicta terra in opere tuo. Et Dominus loquitur Abrahæ: Maledicam maledicentibus tibi. Hac specie maledicendi viri sancti utuntur, ut quum Petrus ait Simoni mago: Pecunia tua tecum sit in perditionem. Atque Elias quarto Regum quinquagenariis dixit: Si homo Dei sum, descendat ignis de cœlo, et consumat vos. Talis est etiam maledictio sancti Job; nec est ira commoti, sed doctrina tranquilli. Vidit quippe amicos flere, et cetera quæ scripta sunt, facere, et inspexit quod hi qui temporalia exquirebant, ex comparatione suæ mentis se temporali adversitate fractum crediderant. Perspexit, quod se transitoria afflictione percussum desperate non flerent, nisi mentem a spe incolumitatis internæ subtraherent: sicque dum erumpit foras in vocem doloris, vulneratis intus ostendit virtutem medicaminis, dicens:
paras.en: [[3:1|After this, Job opened his mouth, and cursed his day|Post hæc aperuit Job os suum, et maledixit diei suo]], [[3:2|And he said|et dixit]]: [[3:3|Let the day perish wherein I was born, and the night in which it was said: A man child is conceived|Pereat dies in qua natus sum, et nox in qua dictum est, Conceptus est homo]]. One must carefully note what is said, [[3:1|After this|Post hæc]], so that the virtue of the thing done may be truly perceived from its time. For first are described the taking away of his goods, the death of his sons, the wounding of his body, the persuasion of his wife, the coming of his friends and what they did, and that they sat there seven days; then is added, [[3:1|After this, Job opened his mouth|Post hæc aperuit Job os suum]], etc., so that by the very order of the narrative it may be weighed that he by no means uttered the curse through impatience. For if he had cursed moved by anger, he would have cursed when the aforesaid troubles were announced and inflicted; yet in them he gave thanks, rebuked his wife, and taught her patience. It was therefore with a quiet mind that he said these things, who even when stricken uttered so many praises of God. Now it must be known that according to Scripture cursing is done in two ways: well, when it is uttered out of zeal or the judgment of justice; and ill, when it is uttered out of the spite of revenge. In the first way the Lord says in Genesis: [[Gen 3:17|cursed is the earth in thy work|Maledicta terra in opere tuo]]. And the Lord says to Abraham: I will [[Gen 12:3|curse them that curse thee|Maledicam maledicentibus tibi]]. Holy men use this kind of cursing, as when Peter says to Simon the magician: [[Acts 8:20|Keep thy money to thyself, to perish with thee|Pecunia tua tecum sit in perditionem]]. And Elias, in the fourth book of Kings, said to the captains of fifty: [[4 Kings 1:10|If I be a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume thee|Si homo Dei sum, descendat ignis de cœlo, et consumat vos]][[4 Kings 1:12||]] [Denis has *consumat vos*, "consume you", the words being said to more than one captain]. Such, too, is the cursing of holy Job; it is not that of a man moved by anger, but the teaching of a man at peace. For he saw his friends weep, and do the other things that are written, and perceived that those who sought after temporal things had believed, judging by their own minds, that he was broken by temporal adversity. He perceived that they would not weep despairingly over him, stricken by a passing affliction, unless they withdrew their mind from the hope of inward soundness; and so, while he breaks out outwardly into a cry of grief, he shows to those wounded within the power of the remedy, saying:

paras.t: Pereat dies in qua natus sum. Quid enim per diem nativitatis, nisi omne hoc tempus nostræ mortalitatis exprimitur? quod quamdiu nos in hac mortalitate tenet, æternitatis nobis incommutabilitas non apparet: quam qui desiderat, ægre diem suæ mortalitatis sustinet. Quid ergo est diei nativitatis maledicere, nisi aperte dicere, Dies mutabilitatis pereat, et lumen æternitatis erumpat? Sed quia perire dupliciter dicitur, primo, ut quod perit, omnino non sit, secundo, ut male sit; hoc, quod de die hoc subditur, Occupet eum caligo, et involvatur amaritudine, clare ostenditur quod dies perire optatur, non ut non sit, sed ut male sit: involvi enim amaritudine nequit, quod omnino non est. Tempus autem tandem omnino non erit, sicque peribit, ut prorsus non sit, sicut in Apocalypsi angelus ait: Quia tempus ultra non erit. Quem ergo vir sanctus nomine diei exprimere voluit, nisi apostatam spiritum, qui in vitali essentia etiam moriendo morte damnationis et culpæ subsistit? Qui optatur ut pereat, quatenus dignis retrusus suppliciis, etiam tentandi licentiam perdat. Qui antiquus hostis, dies est per naturam bene conditus, et prospera promittendo, atque in angelum lucis se transfigurando; sed nox est per demerita ad tenebras lapsus, et ad adversa perducendo ac animas obscurando. Job ergo in dolore proprio causam totius humani generis deflens, et nil speciale in speciali suo vulnere cogitans, reducat ad animum culpam originalem, et dicat: Pereat dies in qua natus sum, et nox in qua dictum est, Conceptus est homo. Ac si aperte dicat: Pereat spes ab apostata angelo illata, qua dixit, Eritis sicut dii: qui ex promissione divinitatis diem se simulans, noctem se exhibuit, lucem nobis nostræ immortalitatis obscurans. Quasi dicat: Pereat antiquus hostis, qui falsam lucem promissionis ostendit, et peccati tenebras contulit.
paras.en: [[3:3|Let the day perish wherein I was born|Pereat dies in qua natus sum]]. For what is expressed by the day of birth, but all this time of our mortality? As long as it holds us in this mortality, the unchangeableness of eternity does not appear to us; and whoever longs for it bears the day of his mortality with difficulty. What, then, is it to curse the day of one's birth, but to say openly: Let the day of changeableness perish, and let the light of eternity break forth? But since *to perish* is said in two ways, first, that what perishes should not be at all, second, that it should be ill: by this, which is added about this day, [[3:5|let a mist overspread it, and let it be wrapped up in bitterness|Occupet eum caligo, et involvatur amaritudine]], it is clearly shown that the day is wished to perish not so that it should not be, but so that it should be ill; for what does not exist at all cannot be wrapped in bitterness. Time, however, will at length not be at all, and so will perish as to be no more at all, as the angel says in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 10:6|That time shall be no longer|Quia tempus ultra non erit]]. Whom, then, did the holy man mean to express by the name of day, but the apostate spirit, who, even in dying the death of damnation and guilt, subsists in a living being? He is wished to perish so that, thrust down into the torments he deserves, he may lose even the licence of tempting. This ancient enemy is a day, as created good by nature, and by promising prosperity, and by transforming himself into an angel of light[[2 Cor 11:14||]]; but he is night, as fallen into darkness by his demerits, and by leading into adversity and darkening souls. Let Job, then, bewailing in his own grief the cause of the whole human race, and thinking of nothing particular in his own particular wound, call original sin to mind and say: [[3:3|Let the day perish wherein I was born, and the night in which it was said: A man child is conceived|Pereat dies in qua natus sum, et nox in qua dictum est, Conceptus est homo]]. As if he said openly: Let the hope perish that was brought in by the apostate angel, when he said, [[Gen 3:5|you shall be as Gods|Eritis sicut dii]]: who, feigning himself day by the promise of divinity, showed himself night, darkening for us the light of our immortality. As if he said: Let the ancient enemy perish, who showed the false light of promise, and brought on the darkness of sin.

paras.t: Dies illa vertatur in tenebras, id est, ab eis qui eam vere diem putabant aut putant, qualis sit, utpote tenebrosa et impia, cognoscatur. Quum enim dæmonem se in angelum lucis transfigurantem, angelum æstimamus, et ea quæ sub specie boni proponit, bona putamus, Satan et ejus tentatio quasi dies est nobis; quum vero cœlitus illustrati recte discernimus, et prava ac ficta qualia sint intuemur, dies in tenebras vertitur. Non requirat eum Deus desuper, id est, apostatam spiritum ad pœnitentiam ac salutem non revocet nec reducat. Quum enim Deus omnipotens duas ad cognoscendum se creaturas fecisset, angelicam et humanam, et utraque per superbiam corruisset, redemit humanam: quoniam carnem habens, in perpetratione culpæ aliquid de carnis habuit infirmitate, et quia non sua sed aliena malitia, scilicet dæmonis machinatione, peccavit: quorum nullum in apostata angelo fuit. Ideo Deus eum ad salutem non requisivit. Et non illustretur lumine gratiæ gratum facientis aut gloriæ; nec unquam lumen pristini status recipiat, quia hoc etiam non suasus amisit.
paras.en: [[3:4|Let that day be turned into darkness|Dies illa vertatur in tenebras]] [a margin note gives the variant reading *Dies ille*], that is, let it be known, by those who thought or think it truly a day, for what it is, namely dark and wicked. For when we take the devil, transforming himself into an angel of light, for an angel, and think good the things he sets before us under the appearance of good, Satan and his temptation are as a day to us; but when, enlightened from heaven, we discern rightly and see what wicked and feigned things they are, the day is turned into darkness. [[3:4|let not God regard it from above|Non requirat eum Deus desuper]], that is, let him not call back or bring back the apostate spirit to penance and salvation. For when almighty God had made two creatures to know him, the angelic and the human, and both had fallen through pride, he redeemed the human: since, having flesh, it had in committing sin something of the weakness of the flesh, and since it sinned not by its own malice but by another's, namely by the devil's contriving; and none of this was found in the apostate angel. Therefore God did not seek him out for salvation. [[3:4|and let not the light shine upon it|Et non illustretur lumine]]: the light of sanctifying grace [*gratia gratum faciens*, the grace that makes one pleasing to God] or of glory; and let him never regain the light of his first state, since he lost it, moreover, without being persuaded by anyone.

paras.t: Obscurent eum tenebræ cæcitatis et obstinationis, et umbra mortis, id est, æternæ oblivioni tradatur. Per umbram enim mortis designatur oblivio, quoniam sicut mors interimit vitam, ita oblivio exstinguit memoriam. Occupet eum caligo erroris, et involvatur amaritudine supplicii gehennalis.
paras.en: [[3:5|Let darkness|Obscurent eum tenebræ]] of blindness and obstinacy [[3:5|and the shadow of death, cover it|et umbra mortis]], that is, let him be given over to everlasting forgetfulness. For by the shadow of death forgetfulness is signified, since as death destroys life, so forgetfulness extinguishes memory. [[3:5|let a mist overspread it|Occupet eum caligo]], the mist of error, [[3:5|and let it be wrapped up in bitterness|et involvatur amaritudine]], the bitterness of the punishment of hell.

paras.t: Noctem illam, id est apostatam hunc vere teterrimum, tenebrosus turbo possideat, id est, ignis conflagrationis et tempestas, quæ in die judicii erit, pertrahant ad infernum. Scriptum est enim: Ignis in conspectu ejus, scilicet Christi judicis, exardescet, et in circuitu ejus tempestas valida. Non computetur in diebus anni, id est inter mentes quibus supernæ gratiæ prædicatio exhibetur, intelligendo per diem, mentem cui lux gratiæ communicatur; per annum, supernæ gratiæ prædicationem, sicut per Isaiam loquitur Christus: Spiritus Domini super me, ut prædicarem annum placabilem Domino. Nec numeretur in mensibus, id est inter particulares electorum Ecclesias, quæ catholicam unam constituunt. Sicut enim ex diebus fit mensis, sic ex pluribus Christi fidelibus resultat Ecclesia.
paras.en: [[3:6|Let a darksome whirlwind seize upon|tenebrosus turbo possideat]] [[3:6|that night|Noctem illam]], that is, this truly most foul apostate: that is, let the fire of the conflagration and the tempest that will be on the day of judgment drag him down to hell. For it is written: [[Ps 49:3|A fire shall burn before him|Ignis in conspectu ejus]], namely before Christ the judge, [[Ps 49:3|and a mighty tempest shall be round about him|exardescet, et in circuitu ejus tempestas valida]]. [[3:6|let it not be counted in the days of the year|Non computetur in diebus anni]], that is, among the minds to which the preaching of heavenly grace is shown; understanding by *day* the mind to which the light of grace is imparted, and by *year* the preaching of heavenly grace, as Christ speaks through Isaias: [[Is 61:1|The spirit of the Lord is upon me|Spiritus Domini super me]], [[Is 61:2|To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord|ut prædicarem annum placabilem Domino]]. [[3:6|nor numbered in the months|Nec numeretur in mensibus]], that is, among the particular Churches of the elect, which make up the one Catholic Church. For as a month is made of days, so the Church is made up of many faithful of Christ.

paras.t: Sit nox illa solitaria, id est, societate hominis, quem tentavit, atque angelico privetur consortio; nec laude digna: imo omni vituperio digna consistit, quæ quum ceciderit, non adjicit ut resurgat, et inconvertibiliter a Deo aversa est.
paras.en: [[3:7|Let that night be solitary|Sit nox illa solitaria]], that is, let it be deprived of the company of man, whom it tempted, and of the fellowship of the angels; [[3:7|and not worthy of praise|nec laude digna]]: nay, it stands worthy of all blame, since, having fallen, it shall [[Ps 40:9|rise again no more|non adjicit ut resurgat]] [the margin reads Ps. xi, 9; the words are those of Ps 40:9], and it is turned away from God past all conversion.

paras.t: Maledicant ei, id est zelo justitiæ, seu rationis judicio, qui maledicunt diei, id est angeli sancti, qui dæmoni diem se simulanti maledixerunt, quando in cœlo peccavit, et cecidit, nuncque maledicunt eidem; qui parati sunt suscitare Leviathan. Leviathan interpretatur, additamentum eorum. Quo nomine Satanas designatur, qui hominibus culpis prioribus alias augere non cessat: quem angeli nunc frenant ac comprimunt; circa diem autem judicii hunc relaxabunt, sicque eum suscitare dicuntur.
paras.en: [[3:8|Let them curse it|Maledicant ei]], that is, out of zeal for justice, or by the judgment of reason, [[3:8|who curse the day|qui maledicunt diei]], that is, the holy angels, who cursed the devil, feigning himself day, when he sinned in heaven and fell, and who curse him now still; [[3:8|who are ready to raise up a leviathan|qui parati sunt suscitare Leviathan]]. *Leviathan* is interpreted *their increase*. By this name Satan is signified, who does not cease to add other sins to men's former ones: whom the angels now rein in and hold down; but about the day of judgment they will let him loose, and so they are said to raise him up.

paras.t: Obscurentur stellæ caligine ejus. Quandoque per stellas virtuosi, æquitate vera splendentes, interdum hypocritæ, qui ante hominum oculos velut magnis operibus lucent, notantur. Hi ergo hypocritæ caligine Satanæ obscurantur, dum in suis erroribus confunduntur, et tales foras hominibus innotescunt, quales intus coram Deo consistunt, videlicet ficti et vani. Exspectet lucem, et non videat. Hoc ad mysticum diaboli corpus refertur, eos videlicet, qui fide, non opere Christiani sunt; et Christum, qui ait, Ego sum lux mundi, exspectant, quem in die judicii hilariter non videbunt, neque secundum divinitatem ipsius. Nec ortum surgentis auroræ, id est splendorem Ecclesiæ electorum, quem in die judicii sortietur, per quem consurget ad lucem æternam beatifice intuendam. Aurora quippe est Ecclesia, quæ pristinæ pravitatis tenebras deserit, seque in novi luminis fulgorem vertit: cujus claritatis exordium et gloriam reprobi non videbunt, quum cœperint in infernum demergi.
paras.en: [[3:9|Let the stars be darkened with the mist thereof|Obscurentur stellæ caligine ejus]]. By stars are meant sometimes the virtuous, shining with true righteousness, sometimes hypocrites, who shine before the eyes of men as if with great works. These hypocrites, then, are darkened by the mist of Satan when they are confounded in their errors, and become known outwardly to men such as they are inwardly before God, namely feigned and vain. [[3:9|let it expect light, and not see it|Exspectet lucem, et non videat]]. This refers to the mystical body of the devil, namely to those who are Christians by faith, not by works; and they expect Christ, who says, [[John 8:12|I am the light of the world|Ego sum lux mundi]] [the margin's numerals are hard to read; the words are those of John 8:12, cf. John 9:5], whom on the day of judgment they will not see with gladness, nor according to his divinity. [[3:9|nor the rising of the dawning of the day|Nec ortum surgentis auroræ]], that is, the splendour of the Church of the elect, which it will receive on the day of judgment, and through which it will rise up to the eternal light, to behold it in bliss. For the dawn is the Church, which forsakes the darkness of its former wickedness and turns itself into the brightness of a new light: the beginning and the glory of whose brightness the reprobate will not see, when they have begun to be plunged into hell.

paras.t: Quia non conclusit, id est, quia aperuit nec clausa reliquit, ostia ventris qui portavit me, id est januam paradisi, ex quo humanum prodiit genus, ubi et conceptio nostra coaluit, hominumque origo, scilicet primus homo, habitavit. Hanc januam diabolus aperuit, dum hominem primum induxit ad culpam, propter quod fuit ejectus. Nec abstulit, id est, auferri mihi non permisit, sed irrogavit, mala culpæ, et ex consequenti mala pœnæ, oculis meis interioribus, seu mihimetipsi. Invidia namque diaboli mors intravit in orbem terrarum.
paras.en: [[3:10|Because it shut not up|Quia non conclusit]], that is, because it opened them and did not leave them shut, [[3:10|the doors of the womb that bore me|ostia ventris qui portavit me]], that is, the gate of paradise, from which the human race came forth, where our conception too took its beginning, and where the origin of men, namely the first man, dwelt. This gate the devil opened when he led the first man into sin, for which he was cast out. [[3:10|nor took away|Nec abstulit]], that is, did not allow to be taken away from me, but brought upon my inward eyes, that is, upon myself, the evils of guilt, and in consequence the evils of punishment. For [[Wis 2:24|by the envy of the devil, death came into the world|Invidia namque diaboli mors intravit in orbem terrarum]].

paras.t: Quare non in vulva mortuus sum? egressus ex utero non statim perii? Cur exceptus genibus? cur lactatus uberibus? Absit nos credere, quod beatus Job tanta scientia præditus, abortivum se optet interisse: sed intus pensanda sunt pondera suæ locutionis. Quatuor etenim modis peccatum perpetratur in corde, et quatuor modis in opere. In corde videlicet suggestione, delectatione, consensu et defensionis audacia. Fit namque suggestio per adversarium, delectatio per carnem, consensus per spiritum, defensionis audacia per elationem. Quatuor etiam modis peccatum in opere consummatur. Primo enim peccatur latenter, deinde aperte sine rubore, tertio per consuetudinem, quarto dum culpa vel nimia præsumptione de divina clementia vel desperatione nutritur. Job ergo humani generis lapsus adspiciat, et quibus præcipitiis mersum sit in foveam iniquitatis perpendat, dicens: Quare non in vulva mortuus sum? id est, cur non solum peccavi primo modo peccandi, sive in corde, sive in opere, ita quod aliis vitiorum modis spiritualiter non obiissem, sicque in vulva, id est in prima suggestione tantummodo, mortuus essem? Egressus ex utero non statim perii? id est, cur ad secundum genus peccati perductus sum? vel cur in illo non potius dumtaxat spiritualiter perii, quam ad tertium malum deveni? Cur exceptus genibus, id est pravis consuetudinibus in vitiis sustentatus, seu tertio modo peccandi adjunctus? Cur lactatus uberibus, id est, audacia defendendi peccatum, seu præsumptione immoderata de misericordia Dei aut desperatione nutrivi me in peccatis, atque ad quartum modum peccandi delapsus sum? Hæc in persona generis humani dicuntur, sicut quod subditur.
paras.en: [[3:11|Why did I not die in the womb?|Quare non in vulva mortuus sum?]] [[3:11|why did I not perish when I came out of the belly?|egressus ex utero non statim perii?]] [[3:12|Why received upon the knees? why suckled at the breasts?|Cur exceptus genibus? cur lactatus uberibus?]] God forbid that we should believe that blessed Job, endowed with such knowledge, wishes he had perished as an untimely birth: rather, the weight of his words must be weighed within. For sin is committed in four ways in the heart, and in four ways in deed. In the heart, namely, by suggestion, delight, consent, and the boldness of defending it. For suggestion comes through the adversary, delight through the flesh, consent through the spirit, the boldness of defence through pride. In deed, too, sin is consummated in four ways. For first one sins secretly, then openly without shame, third by habit, fourth when the sin is nourished either by excessive presumption on the divine clemency or by despair. Let Job, then, look upon the fall of the human race, and weigh down what precipices it has been plunged into the pit of iniquity, saying: [[3:11|Why did I not die in the womb?|Quare non in vulva mortuus sum?]] that is, why did I not sin only in the first way of sinning, whether in heart or in deed, so that I should not have died spiritually by the other ways of vice, and so should have died in the womb, that is, in the first suggestion only? [[3:11|why did I not perish when I came out of the belly?|Egressus ex utero non statim perii?]] that is, why was I brought to the second kind of sin? or why did I not rather perish spiritually in that alone than come to the third evil? [[3:12|Why received upon the knees|Cur exceptus genibus]], that is, sustained in vices by wicked habits, or joined to the third way of sinning? [[3:12|why suckled at the breasts|Cur lactatus uberibus]], that is, why did I nourish myself in sins by boldness in defending sin, or by immoderate presumption on the mercy of God, or by despair, and fall into the fourth way of sinning? These things are said in the person of the human race, as is what follows.

paras.t: Nunc enim dormiens, dormitione quietis beatæ, silerem ab inquietudinibus vitæ præsentis, eis carendo, et somno meo, qui est felix obdormitio mentis in Deo, requiescerem cum regibus et consulibus terræ, id est cum angelis sanctis, per quos Ecclesia militans regitur, optimisque consiliis per internos instinctus docetur et admonetur. Si enim homo præfata non incidisset peccata, non sustineret mala pœnalia, quæ in illorum ultione constat inflicta: siquidem originale peccatum, totius nostræ afflictionis fuit origo. Qui ædificant sibi solitudines, id est, in illo uno quod solum necessarium est, mentis mansiones defigunt, nec quidquam distrahentiæ patiuntur: quia etsi circa plura versantur, cuncta tamen ad unum sine evagatione animi ordinant; sicque in solitudinibus mentis sunt, id est in liberrimis abstractionibus ab omni impedimento pluralitatis, contemplationem beatificam impedientis. Omnes autem qui vel illicita appetunt, vel in hoc mundo videri aliquid volunt, densis cogitationum tumultibus in corde premuntur. At contra sancti viri, quoniam nihil hujus sæculi appetunt, nullis in corde tumultibus comprimuntur: omnes quippe inordinatos desideriorum motus, a cubili cordis manu sanctæ considerationis ejiciunt; et quia transitoria cuncta despiciunt, ex his nascentes insolentias cogitationum non patiuntur: solam namque æternam patriam appetunt; et quia nulla hujus mundi diligunt, magna mentis tranquillitate fruuntur.
paras.en: [[3:13|For now I should have been asleep|Nunc enim dormiens]], with the sleep of blessed rest, [[3:13|and still|silerem]] from the disquiet of the present life, being free of it; and [[3:13|in my sleep|et somno meo]], which is the happy falling asleep of the mind in God, I [[3:13|should have rest|requiescerem]] [[3:14|with kings and consuls of the earth|cum regibus et consulibus terræ]], that is, with the holy angels, by whom the Church militant is ruled, and is taught and admonished with the best counsels through inward promptings. For if man had not fallen into the aforesaid sins, he would not suffer the penal evils which, it is plain, were inflicted in punishment of them: since original sin was the origin of all our affliction. [[3:14|who build themselves solitudes|Qui ædificant sibi solitudines]], that is, they fix the dwellings of their mind in that one thing which alone is necessary[[Luke 10:42||]], and suffer no distraction at all: for although they are busied about many things, they yet order all of them to the one without wandering of mind; and so they are in solitudes of the mind, that is, in the freest withdrawal from every hindrance of multiplicity, which hinders blessed contemplation. But all who either desire unlawful things, or wish to be seen as something in this world, are oppressed in heart by dense tumults of thoughts. Holy men, on the contrary, since they desire nothing of this world, are pressed by no tumults in the heart: for by the hand of holy consideration they cast out of the chamber of the heart all disordered movements of desire; and because they despise all passing things, they do not suffer the insolent thoughts that spring from them: for they desire only the eternal fatherland; and because they love nothing of this world, they enjoy great tranquillity of mind.

paras.t: Aut cum principibus qui possident aurum, et replent domos suas argento. Principes isti sunt efficaces rectores Ecclesiæ, qui domos conscientiarum suarum per aurum, id est sapientiam, ditant, easque argento, id est sacris Scripturarum implent eloquiis. Quod enim per aurum sapientia denotetur, Salomon testatur, dicendo: Thesaurus desiderabilis in ore sapientis. Joannes quoque in Apocalypsi: Suadeo tibi emere aurum ignitum probatum: quod per obedientiam emitur, prout in Ecclesiastico scriptum est, Fili, concupiscens sapientiam, serva mandata, et Deus præbebit illam tibi. Quod vero sacra eloquia per argentum signentur, Psalmista docet, concinens: Eloquia Domini eloquia casta, argentum igne probatum.
paras.en: [[3:15|Or with princes, that possess gold, and fill their houses with silver|Aut cum principibus qui possident aurum, et replent domos suas argento]]. These princes are the effective rulers of the Church, who enrich the houses of their consciences with gold, that is, with wisdom, and fill them with silver, that is, with the sacred words of the Scriptures. For that wisdom is denoted by gold, Solomon testifies, saying: [[Prov 21:20|There is a treasure to be desired|Thesaurus desiderabilis in ore sapientis]] [Denis, following Gregory, reads "a treasure to be desired is in the mouth of the wise" (*in ore sapientis*), where the Vulgate goes on "and oil in the dwelling of the just"]. And John in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 3:18|I counsel thee to buy of me gold, fire tried|Suadeo tibi emere aurum ignitum probatum]]: and it is bought by obedience, as it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 1:33|Son, if thou desire wisdom, keep justice, and God will give her to thee|Fili, concupiscens sapientiam, serva mandata, et Deus præbebit illam tibi]] [Denis reads *serva mandata*, "keep the commandments", where the Vulgate has "keep justice"]. And that the sacred words are signified by silver, the Psalmist teaches, singing: [[Ps 11:7|The words of the Lord are pure words: as silver tried by the fire|Eloquia Domini eloquia casta, argentum igne probatum]].

paras.t: Aut sicut abortivum absconditum non subsisterem. Per abortivum intelligit electos qui a principio mundi ante Christi adventum fuerunt, et tamen scriptam legem non habentes, per legem naturalem Deum timere, et mundo ac voluptatibus se mortuos exhibere curaverunt: qui et absconditi referuntur, quia quum multi valde exstiterunt, paucorum ad nos devenit notitia. Cum his, si non intervenisset transgressio, quievisset vir sanctus, nec in vitæ hujus substitisset tantis miseriis. Vel qui concepti non viderunt lucem. Per quos intelligit patres veteris Testamenti, qui per legem scriptam spiritualiter Deo concepti, sive ad Christum dispositi, lucem tamen quæ est Christus, in carne assumpta corporaliter non viderunt. De quibus ipsemet in Evangelio ait discipulis: Multi justi et Prophetæ voluerunt videre quæ videtis, et non viderunt.
paras.en: [[3:16|Or as a hidden untimely birth, I should not be|Aut sicut abortivum absconditum non subsisterem]]. By the *untimely birth* he means the elect who lived from the beginning of the world before the coming of Christ, and who, though they had no written law, took care by the natural law to fear God and to show themselves dead to the world and its pleasures. They are also called *hidden*, because, though there were very many of them, knowledge of only a few has come down to us. With these the holy man would have rested, had transgression not come between, and he would not have remained in the great miseries of this life. [[3:16|or as they that, being conceived, have not seen the light|Vel qui concepti non viderunt lucem]]. By these he means the fathers of the Old Testament, who through the written law were spiritually conceived to God, or disposed towards Christ, and yet did not see with bodily eyes the light which is Christ, in the flesh he took. Of them he himself says to his disciples in the Gospel: [[Matt 13:17|many prophets and just men have desired to see the things that you see, and have not seen them|Multi justi et Prophetæ voluerunt videre quæ videtis, et non viderunt]] [the margin's reference is unreadable; Denis's *voluerunt*, "desired", is the wording of Luke 10:24, but the just men are named only in Matt 13:17].

paras.t: Ibi, videlicet in luce seu Christo, impii, id est gentiles per apostolicam prædicationem conversi, cessaverunt a tumultu vitiorum pristinæ gentilitatis. De quibus in libro Sapientiæ legitur: Neque vitam neque nuptias mundas custodiunt, sed alius alium per invidiam occidit, aut adulterans contristat; et omnia commixta sunt, sanguis, homicidium, furtum, fictio, corruptio, infidelitas, turbatio, perjurium, tumultus, bonorum Domini immemoratio, animarum inquinatio. Et ibi requieverunt, id est, in onere Christi levi et jugo ejus suavi, fessi robore, id est a propria fortitudine deficientes, et in solo Dei auxilio confidentes. Quibus clamat Christus lux vera: Venite ad me, omnes qui laboratis et onerati estis, et ego reficiam vos; et invenietis requiem animabus vestris. Hi ergo divinis obediendo præceptis, in virtutum actibus, in exspectatione et contemplatione cœlestium, in supernæ visitationis consolatione et gratia dulciter conquiescunt, a se ipsis deficientes, atque in Deo convalescentes.
paras.en: [[3:17|There|Ibi]], namely in the light, that is, in Christ, [[3:17|the wicked|impii]], that is, the gentiles converted by the apostolic preaching, [[3:17|cease from tumult|cessaverunt a tumultu]]: from the tumult of the vices of their former heathenism. Of these we read in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 14:24|they neither keep life, nor marriage undefiled, but one killeth another through envy, or grieveth him by adultery|Neque vitam neque nuptias mundas custodiunt, sed alius alium per invidiam occidit, aut adulterans contristat]]; [[Wis 14:25|And all things are mingled together, blood, murder, theft, and dissimulation, corruption and unfaithfulness, tumults and perjury, disquieting of the good|et omnia commixta sunt, sanguis, homicidium, furtum, fictio, corruptio, infidelitas, turbatio, perjurium, tumultus, bonorum]], [[Wis 14:26|Forgetfulness of God, defiling of souls|Domini immemoratio, animarum inquinatio]]. [[3:17|and there|Et ibi]] they [[3:17|are at rest|requieverunt]], that is, in the light burden of Christ and his sweet yoke[[Matt 11:30||]], [[3:17|the wearied in strength|fessi robore]], that is, those who fail in their own strength and trust in the help of God alone. To them Christ, the true light, cries: [[Matt 11:28|Come to me all you that labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you|Venite ad me, omnes qui laboratis et onerati estis, et ego reficiam vos]]; [[Matt 11:29|And you shall find rest to your souls|et invenietis requiem animabus vestris]]. These, then, obeying the divine commandments, rest sweetly in works of virtue, in the expectation and contemplation of heavenly things, in the consolation and grace of visits from above, failing in themselves and growing strong in God.

paras.t: Et quondam vincti, id est, qui aliquando vitiorum vinculis stringebantur, Salomone dicente: Iniquitates suæ capient impium, et funibus peccatorum suorum constringetur; pariter, ibi requieverunt, sine molestia: quod fit, dum carne mortali quæ aggravat animam, et deprimit sensum multa cogitantem, relicta, ad lucem beatificæ visionis pertingunt, ubi jam nulla esse potest molestia. Non exaudierunt vocem exactoris, id est, suggestioni non consenserunt dæmonis tentatoris, qui humano generi in paradiso semel scilicet nummum deceptionis contulit, et ab hoc quotidie expetere mortis debitum non desistit.
paras.en: [[3:18|And they sometime bound|Et quondam vincti]], that is, those who were once held fast by the chains of vices, as Solomon says: [[Prov 5:22|His own iniquities catch the wicked, and he is fast bound with the ropes of his own sins|Iniquitates suæ capient impium, et funibus peccatorum suorum constringetur]]; [[3:18|together|pariter]] they are at rest there, [[3:18|without disquiet|sine molestia]]. This comes about when, leaving behind the mortal flesh which [[Wis 9:15|is a load upon the soul|aggravat animam]], and [[Wis 9:15|presseth down the mind that museth upon many things|deprimit sensum multa cogitantem]], they reach the light of the beatific vision, where there can be no disquiet any more. [[3:18|have not heard the voice of the oppressor|Non exaudierunt vocem exactoris]], that is, they have not consented to the suggestion of the devil, the tempter, who once, in paradise, lent mankind the coin of deceit, and from then on does not cease daily to demand back the debt of death [the Latin *exactor* is a collector of debts or taxes].

paras.t: Magnus et parvus ibi sunt: quia in requie Beatorum luceque Christi superiores et inferiores, perfectiores et minus perfecti consistunt, qui ibi differunt gradibus præmiorum, sicut hic differebant gradibus meritorum. Propter quod ait Salvator: In domo Patris mei mansiones multæ sunt. Et servus liber a domino suo: id est, qui in hac vita quandoque servivit peccato, et subditus fuit iniquo, conversusque pœnitentiam egit condignam, ibi liber est ab hoc infelici dominio: nihilo minus manet in eo memoria culpæ aliquando habitæ et commissæ. Si enim nulla ibi homo peccati sui memoria tangitur, unde ereptum se lætatur? aut quomodo gratias agit Deo de venia sibi concessa? Sed sciendum, quia sicut nunc sæpe tristium læti reminiscimur, videlicet pristinæ infirmitatis tempore sanitatis, ita tunc transactæ nequitiæ sine læsione beatitudinis recordabimur.
paras.en: [[3:19|The small and great are there|Magnus et parvus ibi sunt]] [Denis puts *great* before *small*]: for in the rest of the blessed and in the light of Christ there are higher and lower, more perfect and less perfect, who differ there in the degrees of their rewards, as here they differed in the degrees of their merits. Hence the Saviour says: [[John 14:2|In my Father's house there are many mansions|In domo Patris mei mansiones multæ sunt]]. [[3:19|and the servant is free from his master|Et servus liber a domino suo]]: that is, he who in this life once served sin and was subject to the wicked one, and then, converted, did worthy penance, is free there from this unhappy lordship. Yet the memory of the guilt he once had and committed remains in him. For if no memory of his sin touches a man there, whence does he rejoice that he has been rescued? Or how does he give thanks to God for the pardon granted him? But we must know that, as now we often recall sad things with gladness, as in time of health we recall a former sickness, so then we shall remember past wickedness without harm to our beatitude.

paras.t: Quare data est misero, id est homini qui se in sæculo isto miserum exsulemque perpendit, et ad patriam sitit ac properat, lux, id est temporalis prosperitas honorisve claritas; et vita, id est, sæculo et hominibus vivere, dominari, præesse, gloriamque humanam habere, his qui in amaritudine animæ sunt? id est, qui bonis doloribus se ipsos afficiunt, peccata lugendo, suum exsilium et patriæ carentiam deplorando: talibus enim molestissimum est vivere mundo, præesse ac honorari, in quantum per hoc a contemplationis quiete præpediuntur, ac diversimode distrahuntur. Electis quoque Deum et superna promissa toto corde quærentibus, suspecta et gravis est temporalis prosperitas, magisque metuunt prospera quam adversa. Quum enim valde occulta sint Dei judicia, dum in hac vita quandoque bonis male est, et malis bene, tunc tamen sunt occultiora, quum et bonis bene est, et malis male. Quum enim bonis male est, hoc contingit ut hic a peccatis suis purgentur, vel gratia ampliori ditentur; aut simili ratione et malis hic bene est, ut pro bonis quæ forte egerunt, nunc remunerentur. At quum bonis hic bene est, et malis male, incertum valde fit, utrum boni idcirco bona accipiant, ut provocati ad aliquid melius crescant, an justo latentique judicio hic suorum operum remunerationem accipiant, ut a sequentis vitæ præmiis inanescant; et utrum malos idcirco adversa feriant, ut ab æternis suppliciis corrigentia eos defendant, an hic eorum pœna incipiat, ut quandoque complenda, eos ad ultima gehennæ tormenta perducat. Quia igitur inter divina judicia gravi incertitudinis suæ caligine humana mens premitur, sancti viri quum sibi suppetere prospera hujus mundi conspiciunt, pavida suspicione turbantur.
paras.en: [[3:20|Why is|Quare]] [[3:20|given to him that is in misery|data est misero]], that is, to the man who regards himself as wretched and an exile in this world, and thirsts for his fatherland and hastens towards it, [[3:20|light|lux]], that is, temporal prosperity or the splendour of honour; [[3:20|and life|et vita]], that is, to live for the world and for men, to rule, to be set over others, and to have human glory, [[3:20|to them that are in bitterness of soul?|his qui in amaritudine animæ sunt]] That is, to those who afflict themselves with good sorrows, mourning their sins and lamenting their exile and their want of the fatherland. For to such it is most irksome to live for the world, to be set over others and to be honoured, inasmuch as by this they are hindered from the quiet of contemplation and drawn this way and that. To the elect, too, who seek God and the promises above with their whole heart, temporal prosperity is suspect and heavy, and they fear prosperity more than adversity. For though the judgments of God are very hidden when in this life it sometimes goes ill with the good and well with the wicked, they are yet more hidden when it goes well with the good and ill with the wicked. For when it goes ill with the good, this happens so that here they may be cleansed of their sins, or enriched with greater grace; or, by a like reason, it goes well with the wicked here, so that they may be rewarded now for any good they may have done. But when it goes well with the good here and ill with the wicked, it becomes very uncertain whether the good receive good things in order that, spurred on to something better, they may grow, or whether by a just and hidden judgment they receive here the reward of their works, so as to come away empty of the rewards of the life to come; and whether adversity strikes the wicked in order that its correction may defend them from eternal punishments, or whether their punishment begins here, so that, to be completed at length, it may bring them to the final torments of hell. Since, then, amid the divine judgments the human mind is weighed down by the heavy darkness of its own uncertainty, holy men, when they see the prosperity of this world at their disposal, are troubled with fearful suspicion.

paras.t: Qui exspectant mortem, id est, quotidie huic sæculo cupiunt funditus mortificari, omnique temporali gloriæ mori, et non venit: quia interdum occulto Dei judicio præesse vel in cunctis occupari honoribus compelluntur: quod tamen ex Dei timore tolerant et inviti; quasi effodientes thesaurum: id est, cum magno fervore mortificationem hanc cupiunt, tantoque fortius, quanto vident suo se fini plus propinquare, quemadmodum effodientes thesaurum, quo profundius foderint, eo ad laborem instantius exardescunt. Gaudentque vehementer quum invenerint sepulcrum, id est contemplationis absconditum et quietis secretum, quo anima absconditur mundo, sicut corpus sepulcro. De talibus scribit Apostolus: Mortui enim estis, et vita vestra abscondita est cum Christo in Deo. Et Psalmista: Abscondes eos in abscondito vultus tui a conturbatione hominum.
paras.en: [[3:21|That look for death|Qui exspectant mortem]], that is, who long daily to be wholly mortified to this world and to die to all temporal glory, [[3:21|and it cometh not|et non venit]]: because at times, by a hidden judgment of God, they are compelled to be set over others or to be taken up with honours of every kind; which they nevertheless bear out of the fear of God, and against their will; [[3:21|as they that dig for a treasure|quasi effodientes thesaurum]]: that is, they desire this mortification with great fervour, and the more strongly the nearer they see themselves come to their end, as those who dig for a treasure are fired to the work the more urgently the deeper they have dug. [[3:22|And they rejoice exceedingly when they have found the grave?|Gaudentque vehementer quum invenerint sepulcrum]] that is, the hiding-place of contemplation and the secret of quiet, in which the soul is hidden from the world as the body is in the grave. Of such the Apostle writes: [[Col 3:3|you are dead: and your life is hid with Christ in God|Mortui enim estis, et vita vestra abscondita est cum Christo in Deo]]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 30:21|Thou shalt hide them in the secret of thy face, from the disturbance of men|Abscondes eos in abscondito vultus tui a conturbatione hominum]].

paras.t: Itaque, cur data est misero lux? utpote viro cujus abscondita est via, id est, qui nescit qualiter vitam suam, quæ via est qua itur ad aliud sæculum, terminabit; qui etiam nescit qualis cras erit; qui etiam nescit an quæ recte agere credit, coram Deo sint vere recta ac placita. Sæpius enim opus nostrum causa est nostræ damnationis, quod putamus esse provectum virtutis; sæpeque Deus ad iram instigatur, unde placari speratur, Salomone dicente: Est via quæ videtur homini bona, et novissima ejus ducunt ad mortem. Et circumdedit eum Deus tenebris prædictæ ignorantiæ et incertitudinis: qui et licet cœlesti desiderio ferveat, quid tamen de eo apud Deum dispositum sit, ignorat. Itaque, cur tali homini lux temporalis prosperitatis arridet, qui sub qua æstimatione sit judicis, nescit?
paras.en: So then: [[3:20|Why is light given to him that is in misery|cur data est misero lux]]? Being [[3:23|a man whose way is hidden|viro cujus abscondita est via]], that is, one who does not know how he will end his life, which is the way by which one goes to the other world; who also does not know what he will be tomorrow; who also does not know whether the things he believes he does rightly are truly right and pleasing before God. For often a work of ours that we think an advance in virtue is the cause of our damnation; and often God is provoked to anger by the very thing by which we hope he is appeased, as Solomon says: [[Prov 16:25|There is a way that seemeth to a man right: and the ends thereof lead to death|Est via quæ videtur homini bona, et novissima ejus ducunt ad mortem]] [the margin gives Prov. xiv, 12; Denis's wording is closer to the same saying in Prov 16:25]. [[3:23|and God hath surrounded him with darkness?|Et circumdedit eum Deus tenebris]] namely, the darkness of the ignorance and uncertainty just spoken of: for though he burns with heavenly desire, he does not know what has been ordained concerning him with God. So then, why does the light of temporal prosperity smile on such a man, who does not know in what esteem he stands with the Judge?

paras.t: Antequam comedam, suspiro. Comedere namque animæ, est supernæ lucis contemplationibus pasci. Suspirat ergo antequam comedat: quia prius gemitu tribulationis afficitur, et postmodum contemplationis refectione satiatur. Nisi enim suspiret, non comedit: quia qui se in hoc exsilio per desideriorum cœlestium lamenta non humiliat, æternæ patriæ gaudia non degustat; et a veritatis pabulo jejuni sunt, qui in hac peregrinationis inopia lætantur. Et quasi inundantis aquæ, sic rugitus meus: id est, vox doloris et lamentationis meæ, quam ex interiori mœrore emisi, magna et vehemens est, quemadmodum aquæ inundantes cum impetu veniunt et tumescunt.
